speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: The questions which are being discussed by these officials are those which were decided at the meetings held at government level last February by federal and provincial heads of government. The amending formula, it was decided then, was not among the priority items. The committee agreed it was more important to try to reach agreement on the substance than on the mechanics of changing that substance, as had been attempted for years and years, so we agreed to reverse the order and that is why the officials are not discussing the aspect to which the hon. gentleman referred.

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister undertake to make a full report to the house in the near future as to the agenda for the meetings of the officials? subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: The agenda can easily be found; it follows from the agenda established in public in front of television cameras last February. I should not like to say more about these discussions at the moment for the simple reason that the provincial and federal governments decided jointly that the officials should hold their discussions in camera and that no public statements should be made.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister not prepared to inform the house precisely as to the agenda which is being discussed?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON MEETINGS OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition should understand that this is not a strictly federal matter. This is being done in co-operation with the provinces. It was decided that these meetings should be private; the provinces have been quite firm in that respect, and I think they are quite right.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said yesterday or the day before, I have written to the provincial premiers to suggest a conference of the Prime Minister and premiers in the second half of November or December. I am still awaiting their answer, but that is the date we suggested.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I wonder whether Canada is going to try to have the United Nations deal with the tragic war in Nigeria?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government, as are all members of this house, is very, very concerned about these tragic events in Nigeria and Biafra. We have been exploring the best means by which the force of public opinion in the world could be brought to bear, and the question of bringing the matter before the United Nations has been considered. As I said in answer to a question the other day, the best way this matter could be brought before the United Nations would be by the neighbouring countries of Nigeria.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Why not by Canada?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The Africans are on the spot, very much concerned, as we are; and I am sure nobody in this house would suggest that we in Canada are more concerned than are the people of the neighbouring countries of Nigeria about the tragic events of these days. If the countries of the Organization for African Unity are not prepared to take an initiative-and we must wait to see-the Canadian government would have no hesitation in bringing before this world body the humanitarian aspects of this conflict.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Why not now?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
There are two questions
involved here. One is that I do not think we should intervene in the political affairs of the people of Nigeria. I do think, however, that we, like all the other people of the world, are concerned with the humanitarian aspects. That is why we have been concentrating our efforts in that direction. I can assure the house that if this were the best way of bringing the matter before the United Nations, the Canadian delegation would not hesitate to take the initiative.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question. Is the minister not aware that the Organization of African Unity has declined to take the initiative at the United Nations, and does this not now free Canada's hands?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is possible to give as definite an answer as that. The Organization of African Unity is still seized of the question and meetings on this question are going on currently in Africa and elsewhere. However, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me most important that we should govern ourselves in terms of how we can be most useful in this situation; not whether we can satisfy our own humanitarian instincts, which are so strong, but how we can act most effectively on behalf of the people of Nigeria and Biafra. This should be the test which should govern all our actions, both in Nigeria and elsewhere.

Unfortunately, as has happened on so many occasions, when the time came to implement this agreement not the Nigerians but the Biafrans turned it down on exactly the same ground, that it would interfere with their military effort.

Some question has been raised as to what has happened to this parliament, what has happened to this house, and why we have not been able to proceed with changes in the rules. I go back to the period with which I am intimately familiar starting in 1964. The record is a sorry, dismal one. Part of the blame may fall upon the house but I submit the greater part must fall on the government.
In 1963 a committee was established. That committee simply met two or three times and said, "There is a problem; we will meet it by setting up a committee next year." In 1964 another committee was set up, a very good committee on which I had the honour to serve with you, Mr. Speaker. It made some very solid, very reasonable, very forwardlooking, fundamental proposals. Those proposals followed many months of discussion, many months of research, many months of meetings, but the sad fate of many of those proposed far-reaching reforms was that they were washed out. The government rejected them.
Then just before the end of that session the government brought in its own measures, which in many instances were inadequate but which to a great extent provided the foundation of the provisional rules under which we operated during the last two years. However, a promise was made that another committee would be set up the following year. Such a committee was set up which met twice and dissolved.
A further committee was set up during the last session of the previous parliament. But it was set up late. It was only established following continuous pressure from this side of the house. But even in the limited time available to it-I think I am justified in saying this-it made some first rate, very substantial proposals not only with regard to far-reaching reforms of a fundamental nature but also with regard to immediate reforms that could be implemented. Several of its proposals were brought in many weeks before the house was finally dissolved but with the holding of the
September 17, 1968

election they went down the drain. Now we find ourselves in our present position.
Because I anticipated this situation, as did other hon. members on this side of the house, during the course of the election campaign I issued a statement on behalf of our party in which I indicated what our approach would be, an approach to which we still hold. I suggested that because of the summary dissolution the proposals then before the house for parliamentary reform had been neatly scuttled and that the harsh atmosphere of an election which spills over into the immediate post-election session of parliament could easily cause delay in getting back to where we were on April 23. I pointed out that many of the rules under which the House of Commons had been operating in the last few years had been provisional, that some did represent an improvement and others had been found by experience to be unsatisfactory. That is still our position today.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The majority of the provisional rules have the approval of members of this party. Others are useless, have been found to be unsatisfactory or have not achieved the purposes for which they were intended. I also point out that we were prepared to consider committees constituted for the duration of a parliament. In this way there would be continuity and the opportunity for members to become conversant with particular subjects. They must also know that the representations and recommendations they made would in fact be presented to the house and would not be held up merely because they were embarrassing to the government. Committees should be reduced in number and the membership lowered. There should be a committee on delegated authority.
I do not have too much time but I must stop here for a moment to emphasize this tremendously important issue. Most of the regulations and most of the authorities which affect the ordinary person in Canada, together with the pressure of large government corporations or crown companies, have come about as a result of authority which this parliament has delegated to others to exercise on its behalf. We live in one of the very few democratic countries that have taken no steps to provide an opportunity for the ordinary man and woman, through the medium of a committee such as I have proposed, to ventilate and bring fourth his argument in respect of
The Address-Mr. Baldwin any grievance he may have which has arisen not because of an act of parliament but because of something done under authority given to others to act under an act of parliament. This has a grave effect on our democratic society. I will not willingly, so far as I personally am concerned, pass over the opportunity for parliamentary reform without something being done about this.
Four years ago I spoke in this house to Right Hon. Lester Pearson, then prime minister. He agreed with me and quoted to me the terms of Lord Hewart's book, "The New Despotism." He said that the government was looking into this problem and would establish some procedure such as a parliamentary ombudsman. He said that they would deal with it in this way. That was four years ago. Nothing has yet been done. I suggest that this opportunity should not be allowed to pass without securing from the government an undertaking to set up a committee. It may well be that the government has other ideas as well, but surely a committee could be set up for a limited period which would have authority not to look into the policy behind the exercise of delegated authority but to look into cases of abuse under delegated authority where it has been used far beyond the extent that was contemplated. This is something which must be rectified at this time.
I see that the time is rapidly passing. I intend to conclude in a few minutes. It may well be that the house will see fit, before Your Honour intervenes, to provide a limited time, which I shall not abuse, for me to conclude the remarks I am making.

I also feel that on an interim basis there must be given to members of the house generally as members, not to the government alone, the right to move that measures be sent to committee before second reading without killing the bill. A feeling is held in many parts of Canada that governments do nothing but govern and that members of parliament are here only to say yes or no to government measures. I disagree with this very violently.
Surely no other body of men and women is better qualified to act as a pipe line or liaison between the people of Canada and the government. Surely the people should have the
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. Baldwin opportunity, through the medium of committees, to bring their views before this house and the government with regard to spending proposals being advanced by the government. Governments must initiate and when the time comes take the final responsibility. I do not for one moment differ with that point of view, but as a result of my experience here, not only as a member of this house but outside, I say that there is a great opportunity for the legislative proposals which are advanced to be moulded, modified and adapted to meet the human needs of the people of Canada and not necessarily the views of those who live in ivory towers in Ottawa. I have seen this happen.
One might look over the list of statutes which have been passed in the last four years. Much more than 50 per cent of these are amending statutes. I admit that it is not possible for a government, even a Conservative government, to anticipate fully all the contingencies and vicissitudes in the conduct of affairs of mankind, but I suggest that many statutes have been ill conceived, badly prepared and badly completed in that they have not been properly, adequately and intimately discussed in this house before leaving here in the finished form. Consequently they are brought back for amendment year after year after year.
I speak, I hope, not only for the members of this party but for all private members when I say that we must be far more intimately concerned with the legislative process and that the government must be prepared to accept this up to a point. I repeat what I said before, that the time must come when a government will say that it cannot accept a proposal because of the financial considerations involved. I am satisfied, however, as much as I have ever been about anything, that there is room and opportunity for the private members of this house to be able to make a much greater contribution to the affairs of government and the legislative spending proposals which affect so deeply and intimately the lives and fortunes of 20 million Canadians.
I conclude by saying that I hope, as I have every reason to, that we will continue our discussions in order to arrive at an interim arrangement. This party has always indicated its willingness to make concessions and has made them. I hope the government will take the same position. I hope and expect that we will include many of the provisional rules, as

we have already indicated. Many of the former provisional rules will have to be carried forward. I hope some of the suggestions I have made will be considered by the government as part of the interim arrangement.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I hope also that a select committee will in fact be set up and that it will be directed by mandatory provision to report back to this house by a given date so that the interim arrangement will disappear. The interim arrangement should be for a specific period. There will then be pressure on the government, the opposition and all hon. members to come forward with permanent changes at least by that time. Time is not on our side. I should like to conclude by quoting what I think is a very important comment by a very distinguished British philosopher who also served his apprenticeship in parliament, in the House of Lords. I refer to Lord C. P. Snow who said:
I can't help thinking of the Venetian republic in their last half century. Like us, they had once been fabulously lucky. They had become rich, as we did, by accident. They had acquired immense political skill, just as we have. A good many of them were tough-minded, realistic, patriotic men. They knew, just as clearly as we know, that the current of history had begun to flow against them. Many of them gave their minds to working out ways to keep going. It would have meant breaking the pattern into which they had crystallized. They were fond of the pattern, just as we are fond of ours. They never found the will to break it.
Mr. Speaker we in this house must find a way to break the pattern into which we have fallen.

The hon. member referred to the fact that it is his party's wish that a time limit be provided with respect to the provisional rules. The hon. member also mentioned that his party would like to arrive at an early agreement this session on reform of the rules. It seems to me still, representing the government, a most reasonable course of action that we should continue on the basis of those rules under which we would have been operating still if, to the regret of hon. members opposite, the house had not dissolved last April. May I suggest that this discussion has not suffered at all from the timetable. I think the hon. member would agree that there has been plenty of opportunity to discuss these proposals. Had they been proposed in July or August, the fact is that there are certain attitudes, perhaps not representative of the hon. member, but representative of members around and behind him, with respect to parliamentary reform with regard to which there may be genuine disagreement.
The third of the proposals put forward was with respect to the committees system itself. As hon. members know, we have at the present time reverted to an antique committees system under the 1962 rules, one which speaks to us from the 19th century. Even the proposals incorporated in the provisional rules have in some respects been found not to be acceptable. It had been the government's intention, and it still is, to find an area which would receive general support. The introduction of changes in the committees system was to reflect clearly the division of responsibility among departments.
The fourth of the propositions we put forward to the house leaders was with respect to the constitution of a special committee on procedure to consider the government's proposals in areas which we felt were the key areas on this question, which committee was to report back to the House of Commons by December 1 recommending not merely certain general outlines with regard to the rules, as the special committee did last session, but also specific changes to the standing orders. That seemed to the government to be a reasonable way to proceed.
We are, as I have said, entirely willing to accept the suggestion made by hon. gentlemen opposite that we should put a specific time limit on this arrangement. That is completely in accordance with the government's wish to proceed with this question with the greatest dispatch possible. But I suggest to the hon. gentleman and his colleagues that a far more rational way of handling the business between now and Christmas would be in accordance with the proposals we have put forward both to deal with supply and to act under the proposals in the provisional rules.
There was a reference in the remarks of the hon. gentleman to the importance of a committee on delegated legislation. He and I have discussed this question. I share his concern about the over-all question of more effective control of our executive and

The Address-Hon. Donald S. Macdonald administrative processes. This concern is shared by myself and the Prime Minister and was the reason for a reference in the Prime Minister's speech to the specific responsibility of considering and recommending to the government certain procedures which might be followed with regard to the effective review, both legislative and legal, of administrative action.

There are a great many possibilities here, such as the British institution of a committee on delegated legislation, setting up an ombudsman system, and the French institution of conseil d'etat. speechtext:
I would agree that this is perhaps a more definite indication of the hon. member's notion of the committee on delegated legislation, and it is a useful suggestion, but I took his term to refer to something similar to the British committee which, as the hon. member knows, does not have the responsibility of suggesting further instruments for administrative review.
The government's general principles with respect to the revision of the rules represent an attempt to deal with a problem which is not unique to this legislature but has been dealt with by all parliamentary legislatures in the commonwealth. Indeed, solutions have been found to the problem both in the United

Kingdom and in sister commonwealth countries long before arriving at one here. It is the problem that in this particular institution, which was founded so closely on the evolution of British party politics in the 18th century, we have a set of procedures which never contemplated both the expansion and the ubiquity of the government in society and the increasing complexity of its problems. I am sure that the hon. gentlemen back in the 18th century would have been amazed to see the intervention of the government in many aspects of human endeavour which were entirely foreign to them then. They would have been equally amazed, to illustrate the second point, at the complexity of questions such as those which parliament will be asked to consider, for example, that of a synchronous communication satellite.
What is involved here is the responsibility of putting through a very large volume of legislation and of doing it in such a way that it can receive the full scrutiny of the elected representatives of the people. It seems clear to the government that the only way to meet these two objectives is by an expanded use of the system of functional standing committees. It would be the government's view-and I have already indicated it in the interim arrangements which we proposed-that the spending estimates of the various departments should be referred, either automatically or, if desired, after debate, to the functional standing committees. In these committees individual members would have the opportunity to confront the minister and leading functionaries of the department and inquire not only into the detailed items of the estimates but also into the broader area of local and private but none-the-less important questions which arise in connection with constituency problems.
It is also proposed-and this was the pattern set forward in the report of the special committee on procedure tabled in March of this year-that in view of the fact that there would not be consideration of estimates in committee of the whole, the number of days to be devoted in the house to purely opposition matters would be stipulated and, as proposed by the special committee on procedure of which the hon. member was a member, that these questions would be dealt with systematically throughout the parliamentary year. In the same way, it is the government's view that just as the detailed examination of the spending estimates requires time and
September 17, 1968

effort on the part of individual members, so the detailed examination of legislation which commonly occurs under our procedure in committee of the whole stage should be dealt with in the functional standing committees of the house so that these committees, which we would hope would build up a certain expertise on these matters over a period of time, could, together with the officials responsible and the minister, propose and deal with amendments and at the same time find opportunities to seek outside opinions by way of evidence from other persons interested in the legislation.
One of the examples cited to me of some success in this role was the manner in which the house dealt in the last session with one of the most complicated and far-reaching provisions in our law, the National Transportation Act. It would be hoped that over a period of time the rule could be established that this should become the general procedure, that is, that the committee of the whole stage would take place in the functional standing committees.
However, it is appreciated that the house as a whole must have the opportunity to consider the questions raised in the standing committee and to cast a final decision on whether or not the recommendations should become the law. Therefore it is proposed that we should not go through the committee of the whole stage once again in the house but that there be a full parliamentary debate on the report of the standing committee, either at the report stage or perhaps on third reading. It is hoped that in time it will be established that this would be the time when the house would really commit itself on whether or not the bill should go forward. It has struck me as an anomaly, which I believe has come about as a result of precedents, that the house should make what is virtually a final declaration with regard to the principle of a piece of legislation at the second reading stage. It seems to me far more logical that this fulcrum point should occur later.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Peace River and I have had an opportunity to have a full miniature debate on this question, and I wonder whether I might be permitted a few more minutes when we resume to complete my remarks, bearing in mind our discussion. If so, may I call it one o'clock?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we rose at one o'clock I had given some indication of the government's intentions with respect to reform of the rules and procedures of parliament. speechtext:
In the case of the ordinary legislative process it would take the place of the committee of the whole, that of course would be after second reading.
In so far as the estimates are concerned the intention would be, after having tabled the estimates, to refer the estimates immediately to the functional standing committees. In making these remarks I should also like to make it clear, as the member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) indicated this morning by his question whether the system would be continued whereby broader questions of public policy could still be considered in committee. We are behind the United States because, basically, we have failed to take advantage of three things. We have failed to make improved and greater use of capital, we have failed to make improved and greater use of advances in livestock technology and we have failed to make improved and greater use of technological advances affecting field crops in recent years.
What have we done to improve the livestock industry? We have turned Canada into a stopping-off place for Charolais cattle. Whatever may be said about this breed I believe it has a part to play in the improvement of our livestock industry. But by making Canada

Mr. Speaker, it is a very humbling experience to have the great privilege of speaking for my first time in Canada's parliament. I wish at the outset to underscore the usual courtesies paid by previous speakers in this throne speech debate to yourself, to the leaders of this house, to the leaders of the parties, to the senior and sophomore members and to the freshmen like myself.
As you know I am the member for Lanark and Renfrew. My riding includes portions of three counties within the Ottawa valley, the county of Renfrew, the county of Lanark and the county of Carleton. I was born in the Ottawa valley and I have lived for 23 of my 33 years within 100 miles of this the nation's capital. As a result I have been privileged on many occasions to sit in the visitors' gallery and gain, by a kind of osmosis, the feel, the
September 17, 19S8

The Address-Mr. McBride cut and thrust, of parliamentary debate. It is thus for me a double honour to be able to take an active part here on the floor of the house itself.
We must always be sensitive to our history. It was a much more brilliant man than I who reminded us many centuries ago that he who is ignorant of what happened before he was born is destined to remain a child forever. I agree. Where we have come from is vitally important in determining where we are going to. Especially is this so if we are to have ourselves, and imbue in our people, any sense of destiny and purpose.
I am well aware also that perhaps everything I say today may have been better said in this house at some earlier date. I do not pretend to have discovered any insights that are uniquely new. Rather, my purpose is to accentuate some of those subjects that I believe need our attention now and in the days and years that lie before us. It seems to me that we are not here to glorify the past but to plan the future. We are not here to reflect the average opinions of the average Canadian but are here to uncover greater possibilities than we have ever yet had.
Our task is one of leadership. I know that Canadians did not elect our esteemed Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because they believed he would follow them. We elected the right hon. gentleman because we know he will lead us and blaze new trails and set new standards for a new age. Similarly, as I look around me today I am convinced that all hon. members in this entire house were sent to parliament because their constituents believed, through the power of the ballot, that they would be the most creative, the most forward looking persons available to come to Ottawa to sculpture the future forms of our beloved nation.
Allow me to set out in both broad and specific terms what I as a novice in the house consider to be the most urgent problems facing us all. It is a cliche to say that we live in a fast moving age. It is also true. As Cardinal Leger used to say, the facts are also the truth. For many people all over the world, the only constant factor is change itself. Rapid social change creates an inevitable sense of rootlessness at the personal level.
Just yesterday we were reminded in this house that in the immediate future people probably will have to enter three different vocations during their lifetime and be educated all over again three different times. We must be aware of the result. It is too easy in

a life of continuous change for the individual to come to believe that he is dispensable, which in a very real sense is true, and experience an increasing sense of loss of any feeling of personal worth and value. Such lowering of one's estimate of one's own innate ability to count for something is the initial cause of the majority of all mental illness. Thus we will and do need as never before in our history to take definite steps to emphasize personal value and the uniqueness of the human dimension.
It seems to me that we must within Canada create and maintain an environment wherein we not only produce persons to work with machines but also persons to work with people. As I said earlier I do not belittle history. But this is a future-oriented age as illustrated by the emphasis upon youth in our culture and even as demonstrated in this house where I, at 33, am some 11 years older than our youngest member.
I, in agreement with the government, want Canada to be a director of the future and not one of its victims. For that reason I am a member of this house. The future, by all indications, will produce an ever-shrinking world. We cannot be isolationistic. We must think of ourselves as citizens of Canada, but we must also think of ourselves as citizens of the world. The day is very near when mere nationalism, if it is that and nothing more, will have a very parochial ring. It is one thing to say that we are among the most fortunate people in the world. Let me give you a devastating quotation:
The rich can only be happy so long as the poor suffer In silence.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Today in a land like Peru a poor peasant woman goes to market down the mountain trail with her chickens and meagre produce piled high upon her head. She has an intimate acquaintance with poverty, disease and illiteracy. Her parents before her were the victims of povery, disease and illiteracy. They assumed that the whole world was poor, diseased and uneducated.
At first sight nothing seems to have changed. This woman's situation is the same as it has been for others for centuries. But there is one thing different and it affects this House of Commons. As she went to market this morning on that far-off mountain trail she likely walked with a very low-cost "transistor radio pressed to her ear. She, unlike her ancestors, knows that all the world is not
September 17, 1968	COMMONS
illiterate, diseased and almost destitute. Her situation is the same but her attitude is changed. The rich can never be happy again because the poor, in an age of mass communication, will never keep silent again.
What does this mean? Our foreign aid has hovered around one half of one per cent of gross national product in recent years, and since the United Nations has recommended that a minimum level of one per cent of gross national product be the target for developed countries it means that if we are to seek a peaceful world and be future oriented we must in a very hard headed way go out across this land and convince the taxpayers that increased foreign aid is not simply the pipedream of some idealist but rather an essential investment in their own children's well-being.
I hope too that we in this twenty eighth parliament can reflect the fact that we live in a pluralistic society. We must, and I believe we will, revise laws restrictive of human rights, for example, laws restrictive of proper family planning, laws which tend to permit the wealthy to attain what the poor are denied. We must reassess, as the throne speech has committed us to do, the lumping together in a legal sense of such diverse chemicals as marijuana and heroin. In short I want, like the Prime Minister, that this be a parliament for the people.
I would, Mr. Speaker, be less than honest to my own integrity if I sat down without mentioning Biafra. In a family the children belong to the parents just as Biafra belongs to Nigeria. In our culture we have assumed for a long time that if the parents to whom the children legally belong brutalize those children, even if they are disobedient and naughty, then the neighbours must take steps for the children's protection. If the neighbours on either side of the home take no action, is the neighbour in the next block thereby excused from taking the most direct and useful action possible for those children's protection? Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the following words:
Like the diet prescribed by doctors, which neither restores the strength of the patient nor allows him to succumb, so these doles that you are now distributing neither suffice to ensure your safety nor allow you to renounce them and try something else.

So spoke Demosthenes 2,300 years ago; yet no words can better describe the plight of the Atlantic provinces today in the light of this throne speech. It was a bitter disappointment, for it followed in the footsteps of the ill-conceived and unfulfilled promises of the Pearson administration that made our area the afterthought area of this nation. This afterthought philosophy persists with the present administration, as exemplified by the statements of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer).
The government acted quickly and without hesitation in announcing a new air policy that will result in the expenditure of $600 million in the construction of two new air terminals for the cities of Montreal and Toronto but offered only the prospects associated with studies of transportation in the Atlantic provinces, plus the ultra-conservative philosophy that dollars and cents will be the determining factor in passenger services that will be available in the future to the residents of the Atlantic provinces, and more especially to the province of Newfoundland.
It is no wonder that the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) rose immediately in this house and asked when the government was going to start cancelling passenger services in the rest of Canada. What other approach could any new member take after hearing that kind of statement from the Minister of Transport regarding a serious problem facing his constituents?
I recommend to the Minister of Transport the words of a great Liberal, the late Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who said more than 30 years ago:
The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.
The voters of the Atlantic area moved in open revolt against an administration that said much but did little. The self-styled despots of the region had little control over the voters, for they had failed to make the federal government recognize their plight. Like Demosthenes, they saw our region as one that could neither survive nor succumb with a government whose every action pertaining to our region was an afterthought.
While the voters of Atlantic Canada witnessed the hysteria that followed the Prime Minister wherever he travelled in this nation, while they heard the words "just society'' and "regional economic disparity" pour forth from

his lips when he spoke, they recalled the utterances of other Liberal leaders and were not deceived. We learned recently that Toronto the good had carried out a special study of the maritimers who come to that great city seeking work. This study group recommended that the city inform federal manpower centres that they require no future citizens from the maritimes. They gave some very uncomplimentary descriptions of those who had migrated in the past. The philosophy which initiated, produced and publicized such a study is reminiscent of that in vogue in Hitler's Germany and is unacceptable and inexcusable in the Canada I know. I say to these Toronto men of warped reason that we are as anxious as they to keep our people in the maritimes and that almost without exception our people desire to remain there. What we require is a drastic change of pace on the part of the federal government, one that will provide the weapons for us to overcome adversity, not the agglomeration which represents today federal government policy in the Atlantic provinces.
We have the great projects which could transform our region from the have not to the have category, but we require action and

September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. Coates imagination on the part of this government. For years we have spoken of the three C's: The causeway, the corridor road and the Chignecto complex. Already this government is preparing the causeway for the guillotine. The mover of this debate has urged the government to give unfavourable consideration to the corridor road, and the Chignecto complex awaits the same fate from a government which up to now has reacted to one study by setting up another.
The Prince Edward Island causeway would be a self-liquidating project based on present federal government expenditures to maintain a transportation link between that province and the mainland. The corridor road has long been promoted as the means of moving our goods much closer to the markets of central Canada, but because this young man, at this early stage of his political career, cannot see beyond his constituency, he counsels the government to kill a project which might well become the cornerstone of a new transportation system for our region.
Naturally I must hope that the foresight of the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) will allow him, with time, to see the problems of the area on a regional rather than a constituency basis. If the causeway and the corridor road face the guillotine, can we anticipate the same fate for the Chignecto complex?
It is my view that the problems of the Atlantic region are so severe as to require daring on the part of the federal government. This means the undertaking of the harnessing of the Bay of Fundy tides as a source of power as soon as the government has the assurance it is feasible from an engineering standpoint. We cannot afford the luxury of an economic debate but rather need the kind of courageous decision for Atlantic Canada that was displayed for central Canada in the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway and for western Canada in the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam.
We are told by the Prime Minister that the government will approach this matter through its manpower policies. If the government persists in this philosophy, the Atlantic provinces will become the training ground for industry in central Canada. Our people will be trained or retrained for non-existent jobs in the Atlantic region and then provided with one-way tickets out of the region. The ghost of Walter Gordon casts its ugly shadow over our area once again.

A new breed of man must appear on the scene in Atlantic Canada. He must be fearlessly determined to protect our area from the afterthought philosophy and from further economic erosion. The 32 members from the Atlantic provinces must become the vanguard of the army at home which will fight for equality and justice. I have had the pleasant experience of meeting a man in the present administration who might well provide enlightened leadership to this vanguard in Ottawa, namely, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Jamieson). I will watch with anticipation his words and actions in the days ahead. If he meets my expectations and if his deep concern for our problems continues, progress is assured.
This new breed of man must generate inspiration to the legions at home so they may fight discrimination and win equality of opportunity, thereby guaranteeing that the words of Demosthenes will not be the epitaph on our tombstone.

Mr. Speaker, as a newly elected member from a newly created riding I am pleased, through the courtesy of my colleagues, to be able to take part in this debate at this time. If I were to say that I did not come here to talk, that statement would be both inaccurate and misleading. It is not, however, how much is said but rather the quality and relevance of what is said that will determine whether this parliament can reverse the trend of electoral drop-outism which is found in an increasing segment of Canadians. It will be my objective, then, to deal with matters before this house in a positive, conscientious way.
Other speakers have offered congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, upon your election to this important office. May I be permitted to add mine, with the observation that last Thursday you advanced to your position from the back row of the opposition benches. I will accept this as a good omen for others in my row interested in upward social mobility, although I doubt that our rise will be quite as rapid.
Laudatory words of congratulation to the right hon. gentleman who is our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have also been extended repeatedly. I hope that in adding my voice to the chorus I will be forgiven if I fail to launch myself into stellar flights of oratory of a kind comparable with those words which have come from the government side of the house. There are three major reasons for my ungrudging but comparatively subdued greeting. First of all, I sit in the opposition, so in that sense my mission here is to bury Caesar, not to praise him. Second, my presence here is not a result of this gentleman's popularity in the recent election. In fact, the contrary is the case and I am here despite it. Finally, but most importantly, much of what has been said in reference to the Prime Minister has implied accomplishment of what is but yet potential. Wishes are not facts; sentiments are not solutions. Good intentions are but pavement on the road; they are never to be confused with progress along it.
This brings me to a crucial point in considering the rather dreary document before us, the speech from the throne. One would have

anticipated a 20th century banner of excitement and verve to be unfurled, an imaginative, courageous blueprint for a new Canada. This is what our country hoped for and deserved, but we did not get it. At a time in our history when pride in ourselves as Canadians was glowing as never before we were ready to be challenged, anxious for the new look and famished for idealistic leadership. But, Mr. Speaker, we were disillusioned. We were served with a skilfully vague reiteration of the status quo when we had every right to expect, from advance notices, a ringing manifesto for social change. This speech will send no one to the barricades, sir-more likely to the rail.
Reform in parliament we can all support, I believe, but it does not necessarily follow that reform in government will be the result. Forms are much more easily amended than substance. People may be fooled for a while by what looks like improvement, but if the "just society" turns out to be "just a front" their revenge may be devastating.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am certain that my constituents, the pensioners, the veterans, the rural poor, the unemployed, the fishermen, the Indians, the educated, the uneducated, the sick, the weary and the discouraged, will all be fascinated to discover how past governments could be accused of concentrating on the distributive aspects of our economy. Only a week ago we received the report of the economic council which sets forth in alarming terms the contradiction that 40 per cent of Canadians are on the short end of the distributive stick. Many people in my riding will give great support to a government willing to give greater concentration to an even better distribution of the wealth of our country. The plain fact of the matter is that, despite our affluence, far too many people in Canada have far too little of the things necessary for hope and happiness and dignity.
The government knows full well that exhortations to work harder, to show more individual initiative, will have little effect on the productivity of the unskilled and unmotivated. Millions of these people struggle now in a circle of hopeless drudgery and inflation is forcing them to run harder just to stay where they are.
Lectures on outmoded economic theories will not help, either. We are short of money to spend on the things we need, like schools,

hospitals, universities, research and retraining, because we have squandered millions on things such as Bobcats, Arrows, Bomarcs and Norads, that we do not need or no longer need.

No, I think the secret of improved productivity lies in improving the skill of the average Canadian; and this implies a massive investment in the human resources of our country, especially in education. Canada is no longer a rural society, although many look back nostalgically to when it was. We are, rather, a nation where fewer than 10 per cent of our people live on farms and the rest now live in urban centres. When we remember too that over half of the parents in this country have only grade 8 education we can then appreciate the tremendous job ahead in transmitting educational values to the young.
John Porter had this to say recently, and I quote it because I believe it to be of great relevance if one wishes to tackle the problem of productivity with diligence. He said:
If a society as it is becoming industrialized fails to upgrade its labour force ... there is an alternative open to it, and that is to go and get its skills some place else, and that is what Canada has done to a great extent. It is quite fair to say that the high level of industrialization which Canada enjoys today rests not only on the importation of foreign capital but on the importation of foreign skills and professions Canada has failed to produce.
The path seems clear then, Mr. Speaker, as to what might be done to begin to improve productivity. Our people are neither stupid nor lazy; too few have had enough education of the right kind. Far from having too much of this free stuff, many have had too little.
The story of the average Canadian is the story of wasted talent because of inadequate preparation to meet the demands of the technological society- Our lag in regard to education can be seen when we recognize that 15 per cent of Canadians have enjoyed postsecondary training compared with over 40 per cent in the United States. Too often, of course, it is not the most able who go on, because the financial demands of higher education are insurmountable to all the most dedicated of the poor.
It is no longer news that a disproportionate number of the sons and daughters of upper income families are to be found in our
The Address-Mr. Rose secondary schools and universities; yet middle and low income groups have the most brain power simply because they contain more people. I believe that this state of affairs is no longer satisfactory. It is too late for such wastefulness. It is the ability to learn, not the ability to pay, which should determine who is to go on.
Now is the time to renounce once and for all the outmoded and inefficient concept that the federal government has no business in education. The national government has already stuck its toe in the water of vocational, agricultural and university education. Now is the time to plunge right in and come up with a bold program. I agree that there is sound constitutional validity that primary and secondary education remain the preserve of the provinces, but there is nowhere near the historical justification for post-secondary institutions of learning to be exclusively under provincial control. At the time of confederation institutions of higher learning were privately endowed and not state supported. It seems to me, therefore, that provincial claims to exclusive rights here are extravagant.
The products of higher education are a natural resource of prime importance. Their mobility, expertise and contribution to our country's development make it essential that a greater interest and investment in postsecondary education be undertaken by the national government. More and more young people are knocking at the doors of these schools and finding them closed. I suggest that this condition can only perpetuate the teach the best, shoot the rest elitism we have traditionally accepted in Canada. More schools must be built and different kinds of schools developed for the vast variety of talents and skills possessed by our youth and to provide an educational alternative to those not wishing to go to colleges or universities. This is a way to increase productivity. Our neighbour to the south has enjoyed outstanding industrial success largely because it has deliberately broadened and democratized its educational system and produced the most skilful work force in the world. The broader the base, the higher the pyramid it can support.
The lack of federal consideration of education is inconsistent with the objectives of a modern state. A patchwork of ten provincial systems each running off in all directions is an extravagance 20 million people can scarcely afford. I propose that a national office of

September 17, 1968
The Address-Mr. Rose education be established, whose functions would include the following: First, to assume leadership in establishing some uniform grade and subject standards across the land, so that children of our mobile work force will no longer be educationally penalized nor psychologically disadvantaged by moving abruptly from one school system to another.
Second, we need a national office of education to stimulate and co-ordinate educational research in Canada so that we will not remain as dependent on the importation of foreign research as we are on foreign capital and skill. Third, we need a national office of education to administer grants, directly to institutions, if necessary, in order to hasten the day post-secondary training and retraining at public expense are considered as much a right as we now accept education to be in the elementary and secondary systems.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I must express my regret that the government has recently allowed a 2 per cent increase in the Canada student loan interest rate. This regressive measure penalizes those who can least afford it. Why has the government not moved in exactly the opposite direction? Why has it not provided more able young Canadians with the kind of incentives it offers university officer candidates for the Canadian forces? I have no objection to paying young people $187 per month to go to university because I know the whole country benefits in the long run. But it does evoke some comment on our priorities that we willingly pay $187 per month to train young men to kill and be killed while we raise the loan rate for future teachers by 2 per cent.
Fourth, we need a national office of education so that no country in the world will be in doubt that the educational address of Canada is not in Victoria, British Columbia or Quebec city but is in the parliament buildings, Ottawa. We must in future avoid a recurrence of the recent controversy and national embarrassment caused by the attempted extraterritorial extension of provincial educational rights. Finally, we need a national office of education to improve and make more meaningful the cultural life of Canadians.
I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the grim technocratic nature of the document before us. It has little or nothing to say about the quality of life to which many Canadians aspire. It comes through to me as having a clinical, sterile, impersonal quality emphasizing efficiency and muscle in an age when
FMr. Rose.]
technology seems on the verge of releasing man for a new renaissance of creation and re-creation. Campus activists who are demanding a greater share in decision making are but the tip of the iceberg of youthful discontent. Many young people find it no longer acceptable to have their educational systems so completely ordered by adults that they are likely to emerge from schools as dehumanized units destined for industrial and commercial oblivion.
What man does with his leisure is largely dependent upon how he was educated. And one of man's greatest new problems is likely to be how to fill in the time between birth and death constructively. It is inconceivable to me that a cabinet led and dominated by Latins could articulate the Puritan ethic more admirably. May I ask: Oh where, oh where, is your Gallic flair?

On the north bank of the river, between the Fraser and Burrard Inlet, is a hilly area commanding a view of the valley. This is the area served by the Coquitlam school district and is the fastest growing urban area in B.C. This is where I make my home. I grew up on the banks of the Fraser and for 35 years of my life have lived within a mile of its shores. It is not only what you know about an area but what you feel about it that is the crucial thing, and I would like to tell this house in the time remaining to me how I feel about a few matters affecting my riding.
For all purposes, and with apologies to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the Fraser valley provides the only corridor to Canada's west coast. In fact the Fraser delta is Canada's Pacific coast. The two major rail lines, a freeway and the river have sought this natural way to the sea. In addition, the best of the 2 per cent of B.C. land suitable for agriculture is found here. Our planners tell us that the population will double by the turn of the century, and today the pressure of subdivision and suburban encroachment on the remaining farm land is reaching alarming proportions.
Joint efforts on the part of Fraser Valley municipal governments toward the solution of regional problems are worthy but are just beginning. The concept of regional planning received a cruel, if not fatal, blow recently by the intrusion of a third rail line right through the middle of some fine farms. This was done against the advice of the planners, against the wishes of municipal governments, and of large numbers of citizens who feel the presence of this B.C. Hydro and Power Authority line to be largely redundant, politically motivated and an affront to good planning. Many people believe, Mr. Speaker, that this new line for unit trains to the federally-financed Roberts Bank superport was located in the best interests of the railroads alone, ignoring recreational and conservational factors. And so do I. Many also believe that if the federal government is not guilty of complicity with the B.C. government in agreeing to the route it is, at the very least, guilty of a weak, waffling posture on the whole matter. And so do I. To take 100 car unit trains of coal up a mountain, through rich farm land and finally along the best bathing beach and waterfowl area in the lower mainland, when there is a reasonable alternative open, is a decision that appears ludicrous.

We are pleased in the valley, on the other hand, that at long last some concrete federal-provincial legislation has appeared designed to overcome the devastation of the periodic Fraser flooding. Certainly those who remember the 1948 flood now have better cause to be optimistic although legislation by itself is seldom watertight enough to protect the land. We shall not quarrel either with the timing of the announcement and visit by the minister himself to my riding during the early weeks of the election campaign; we must agree that progress in this problem of flood control is now possible. I do submit, however, that dikes are relatively temporary measures and the permanent solution to Fraser flooding probably lies in controlling the run-off by means of storage dams in the Fraser canyon.
A very serious problem confronting my riding also concerns the waters of the Fraser and its tributaries and Burrard Inlet too. With the pressure of expanding population and the limited means available to municipalities to raise revenue, it is almost inevitable that our waters be gradually polluted. Raw sewage is a distinct problem in Burrard Inlet as is the spillover of sulphur from the Canadian Pacific bulk loading facility. Fraser fishermen at Fort Langley tell me it is now possible to ascertain when the people 20 miles upriver at Mission City have eaten asparagus for dinner. Moreover, the Coquitlam river, an excellent sports fishing stream, is constantly being despoiled by the activities of gravel companies whose depredations along its shores have at places turned it into a Hollywood set suitable for a life on the moon series. Much more federal leadership in the standards and control of pollution is vital if we are to avoid poisoning ourselves, and I await with much interest and anticipation the specifics to follow from the reference in the speech from the throne to conservation of our resources.
I should be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not bring before this assembly on behalf of the municipalities I represent their concern for the manner in which the winter works program was guillotined. The explanation given by the government that the program was not the most effective way of using funds may contain some measure of truth, but to suggest that manpower training programs can immediately replace winter works is a statement which completely boggles the mind. If winter works were to be discarded at a time

My government intends to press forward its plans and programs for international co-operation and development which includes the establishment in Canada of an international development centre.

catch the industrially developed. If we are not successful in lessening these disparities and solving these problems, we will have lost the race with disaster, Mr. Speaker, and whatever else we may do here becomes irrelevant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just as previous speakers, allow me to offer you my heartfelt congratulations on your election. Before I begin my speech, I would like to make a small correction concerning the title given to you. In French, an "orateur" is one who delivers speeches before a meeting or a very eloquent man, while a "president" is the person who conducts the proceedings of a meeting or a court, according to the definition of the Larousse dictionary. I will take the liberty during my speech to call you in French "monsieur le President".
Mr. Speaker, allow me first to congratulate warmly the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette).
Since Thursday last, I have experienced my first hours as a member in the House of Commons. And we knew the most serious and pleasant moments Monday evening, September 16, when the hon. member for Temiscamingue took part in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the unusual attention then prevailing in the house was an indication of the good faith of its members and an encouragement for the 400,000 electors who supported the Ralliement Creditiste.
Mr. Speaker, like all my colleagues, I approve the subject of the Speech from the Throne: the establishment of a just society. We now have to discuss the means to be taken so as to establish that just society.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) certainly indicated in his answer to the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that the time for good intentions was past. I am very glad to hear it, Mr. Speaker, but I am afraid it may only be the same old story which all government leaders have told over the years, as the hon. member for Temiscamingue so well demonstrated in his speech.
It is time, Mr. Speaker, to think of passing concrete measures to solve the problems facing the Canadian people. Let us stop talking about problems and find solutions. To make financially possible what is physically possible
September 17, 1968

is not an empty election campaign promise. I am ready, Mr. Speaker, to support any government measure which would put credit or money at the service of the citizen. This system proved itself in wartime. The billions of dollars put into circulation in the form of credit during the period 1939-45 started an era of prosperity which continued even for a few years after the war, in fact until we applied again those famous restraints which result only in making the rich richer and the poor poorer.
As a matter of fact, we simply want a just society. We want every citizen to be reasonably well off. We want a fair distribution of all the riches of our country. We want all Canadians to be equal culturally, while being equal financially, with a vital financial minimum.
This brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the main topic of our times in Canada, and even sometimes abroad, the situation of Quebec within Confederation and the problem of the existence of the French-Canadian nation in this vast country of ours.
To wish for the emancipation and the complete fulfilment of one's nation can hardly be considered as a violation of the national integrity of any country. When I said to the people of the Champlain riding that I would champion the rights of Quebec in Ottawa, I was simply doing my duty as a responsible citizen who wants to contribute to the expansion of the whole country through the complete development of the characteristics which Providence has deigned to bestow upon us.
Quebecers or French-Canadians do not have any animosity or hatred against their compatriots of other origins. It is unfortunate that their sincere desire towards emancipation and improvement is often interpreted as something negative, if not destructive.
The example of the difficulties in Saint-Leonard shows very well the rather odd situation existing in Quebec, particularly in the greater Montreal area, where 90 per cent of the immigrants are being assimilated by the English-speaking community. If I decided to live in Spain, it seems to me obvious that I would have to adopt the Spanish culture, as well as I would have to become Russian if I were to settle in Russia. Why then should the Italian, Portuguese, or German who settle in Quebec not accept to become Quebecers?
The Address-Mr. Matte
Furthermore, the federal government should assist in the integration of those immigrants into the Quebec French-speaking community. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because, if the present pace is maintained, in view especially of the progressive, and even alarming, decrease of the birth rate in the province of Quebec, we cannot be sure that Frenchspeaking Quebecers will still form a majority in Quebec 15 or 20 years from now. It is understandable why we think of self-preservation, when we have to answer the question: "What does Quebec want?'' Canada as a whole should not contribute to that new-style genocide whereby a nation would slowly waste away unnoticed by its political elite which is present here, in this house, precisely in order to safeguard the fundamental rights of the nation.
I am sure, as was so rightly said one day by a certain general, that whatever the problem, time will provide a solution, on condition we stop, as soon as people express pro-Quebec feelings, placing them in a priori categories and interpreting their position as a stand against Canada.
Now, may I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to underline an abnormal situation concerning the very foundation of a just society, namely a provision of the Military Voters Act.
After my election, a judicial recount was held in the riding of Champlain, and I thus had the opportunity to see for myself the anti-democratic character of this vote. I understand, Mr. Speaker-and I congratulate our armed forces officers-that our soldiers are very well trained. They file past in step, they eat together, they follow together a hard and formative discipline. But I would never have believed that this discipline was so strict as to compel all our soldiers to write the same.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, on checking the registered military vote in the riding of Champlain, to our surprise and later to our merriment, in which the astonished presiding judge finally joined us, all the voting papers bore identical signatures in favour of the candidate of the party in power.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the same rules should apply to the vote of the military as well as to that of the other citizens. I would therefore suggest:
(1)	That the list of the military in a riding be posted like the ordinary voters list.

September 17, 1968
The Address-Mr. Matte
(2)	That the military should vote at the same time as the other voters and that those who are stationed away from home not be prevented from voting in the temporary polling booths set up across the country.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
(3)	That they use voting papers identical to the ones used by the other voters and not the small yellow slips on which they write the name of the candidate for whom they wish to vote.
(4)	That all the military vote in a single riding set up expressly for them, or else in the ridings where they have in fact a home.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let there be an end to the vote of the unknown soldier.
Here are a few suggestions which could be applied immediately to improve the lot of the population of the Champlain riding. That huge riding which stretches along the St. Lawrence river, from Portneuf to Ste-Mar-the-du-Cap-de-la-Madeleine, and extends as far north as Parent, that is some 250 miles, has heterogeneous interests.
The southern part of the riding is made up mostly of farm parishes. One knows, Mr. Speaker, that in Quebec, where there are so many paradoxical things, the farmer who is called upon to feed the people is hard put to feed himself. The satisfactory solution would be to guarantee the purchase of all his production, and until that policy is established by the Quebec government, the federal government should be much more generous in granting subsidies.
With regard to the other workers as a whole, it seems rather funny to them that those who strike already make two or even three times as much money as they earn as a rule. Many more municipalities should be considered as designated areas in order to get help that would enable them to improve their economy.
The people of the northern part of my riding are particularly concerned about another problem. From La Tuque to Parent, all the inhabitants or workers-there are a few thousands-are deprived of television coverage. It seems to me that is an injustice, the more so as these isolated people are in greater need than others of excellent information and recreation media.
Radar towers which are now placed 25 miles apart as far as Parent could be used right away. So, with hardly any coats, these

people could enjoy television, which is an indispensable thing nowadays.
The northern part of the riding of Champlain is not the North Pole after all, and it is unthinkable that in 1968, this everyday service has not yet been extended there.
Another suggestion, Mr. Speaker. It is about the implementation of a plan already submitted to the government concerning the establishment of a rehabilitation centre on the former radar base at Parent. I visited the site last summer and I found it disgraceful that such a place which cost some twenty million dollars is left in utter neglect while it could easily be converted into a rehabilitation centre. The establishment of such a centre would enable the development of a whole area.
We can only hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will consider these few remarks or suggestions, and you can rest assured that I will heartily co-operate in any endeavour leading to a just society.
