speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words are to join with other hon. members in extending congratulations to you, who we hope will be our permanent Speaker, and to join with those who have extended congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply.
In rising to take part in this debate I have no desire to burden hon. members with further criticisms of the speech from the throne. I believe the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) dealt with it adequately. He dealt with its shortcomings as did other hon. members. Suffice it to say it was a flatulent restatement of things already done, a poor statement of policy for a just society, and a great disappointment to the people of Canada who expected much more from this new government.
It was only exceeded by the Prime Minister's vain attempt in his speech in this debate to try to explain it. If these speeches, the speech from the throne and the Prime Minister's speech, are to be our first full measure of what the just society is, then we can only pray for its demise.
There is only one more observation I should like to make before I leave the subject of the speech from the throne. I have in mind the fact that this is the first time in the history of our country a Canadian government has been forced to apologize in advance for its failures. Usually they have been able to wait
September 17. 1968	COMMONS
two, three or even four years before explaining or attempting to alibi their legislative and administrative shortcomings. Great expectations have already dwindled to puny expectations.
I would be happy to let the speech from the throne quietly die, were it not for a phrase that runs through it like a refrain-its only distinguishing aspect. That phrase is the one we have heard much of since this debate started. I refer to the much heralded "just society". I find this choice of words by the Prime Minister to describe his new Canada disappointing to the people who look for a bold new approach to government by a government that was to fire the imagination of young Canada.
I find it offensive when I think of my native province, and when I think of my constituents in this context. It is a hollow mockery of the phrase "the just society" when there are Canadians in this country today living in socially and economically unjust conditions, aggravated, if not indeed produced, by the past neglect and the very indifference of the people who now join in the alleluiah chorus and talk about the just society.
In my opinion no political party and no Canadian government carries a greater share of responsibility for the social and economic injustice so prevalent in this country today than does the Liberal party and the government of this country. Ask the people of Atlantic Canada. Ask the people of Newfoundland. Ask the people of my city, my constituency. Ask the 6,500 Canadians who still live without hope and in despair in the mining town of Bell Island. This industrial community, the oldest in Newfoundland and one of the oldest in eastern Canada, was the scene of an iron ore mining operation carried on successfully since the turn of the century. These operations were curtailed in 1963 by A. V. Roe, placing out of work over 1,400 people, their dependants, and those who worked in service industries.
At that time these people looked for justice to the new government of that day. At that time it was not the just society; it was the war on poverty. Well, we still have the injustices of poverty in this country. After the war on poverty we now have the just society. The people of Newfoundland did not buy it. They defeated six Liberal candidates who sat in this last parliament because they know it is too late to try to excuse the neglect of the past five years with empty catch phrases. The people of Bell Island today live in despair.
DEBATES	133
The Address-Mr. McGrath They live without hope. They live under the cruel soul shattering, morale destroying, welfare which is today their lot. They are not permitted to work. They are not permitted to retain their pride by working for a living, because under the provisions of the Canada Assistance Act which grants funds to the provinces for relief purposes they are not permitted to work for their welfare. Our people want work and they want to hold their heads up and work for what is just and rightly theirs.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
For too long, Mr. Speaker, the government of this country has been content to close its eyes to the urgent social and economic problems and needs of the Atlantic provinces. For too long the government has been content to close its eyes to the serious problems facing Canada's tenth province. The government has been content to sit silently in this house and allow Newfoundland to remain the sealed off personal fief of Joey Smallwood, in return for a solid seven Liberal members and supporters.
Times have changed and our people want a better deal. The man who likes to refer to himself as the only living father of confederation is tottering on his throne. The people of my province have rebelled against 20 years of neglect and injustice. Mark my words, they want their place in this just society. They feel they are entitled to a place in this just society, if there is to be one. They looked with hope in 1949 for a just society that never materialized.
I could find no such reference in the Prime Minister's book "Federalism and the French Canadians". I should like to read from page 68, so you can see if there is something missing from my concept of what this phrase means:
-the continued complaints of the maritimes finally won them preferential treatment in 1932-
He writes about preferential treatment for the maritimes in 1932, but this is the key phrase:
-and last, in 1949, Newfoundland made the federal government pay dearly for its entry into confederation.
This is what the Prime Minister wrote. But if this is the just society that we are to expect from this new administration, then the people of Atlantic Canada, certainly the people of my province, want no part of it.
134	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. McGrath
Is it a just society that would allow the Shaheen deal to go through? I refer to the deal concluded by the Newfoundland government with the Shaheen group whereby the government of Newfoundland has deprived the people of Newfoundland from their birthright. That government has made it possible for this New York financier to buy up for a mere $2,000 the entire untaxed profits earned over a 15 year period of a provincial crown corporation.
Who is to speak for the people of Newfoundland in this just society? This financier has accomplished this fantastic deal without risking one penny of his own. The deal has been called many things, two cabinet ministers resigned from the Newfoundland government because of it, and the throne man of Newfoundland is tottering because of this and other abuses. Suffice it to say this is a monument to the folly of unchallenged Liberal power in Newfoundland and is a gross perversion of the intent of crown corporation legislation.
What will the federal government do about this situation? What about the new minister from Newfoundland, whom I congratulate on his appointment to the cabinet-what will he do? The people of Newfoundland look to him for a fair measure and share of the justice we have heard so much about.
In any event the people of my province have been cheated in such a blatant fashion there is a moral obligation on the government of Canada to do something about these things. The people of my province are justly concerned about the abuses that are still carried out in the name of government. The only real evidence we have seen of the just society, if indeed one can continue to term it such, has been the cancellation of programs by this government. In the midst of the fishing season the salt rebate program was cancelled, without even any suggestion of what is to replace it. This has caused hardship to hundreds, yes, even thousands of Newfoundland and maritime fishermen who depend upon this salt rebate as a means of increasing their already meager earnings.
We have seen the evidence following the cancellation of the winter works program. This will result in great hardships to the cities of the Atlantic provinces, indeed to the cities of Canada, but especially to the cities and municipalities in my province which already suffer from the highest rate of unemployment in all of Canada. This program was

DEBATES	September 17, 1968
cancelled without even a vague suggestion of a replacement for it.
What reference is there in the speech from the throne to this very serious crisis facing the fishing industry in Newfoundland today? This is an industry from which 150,000 Canadians directly or indirectly derive their livelihood, an industry which in economic terms represents almost 3 per cent of the gross national product in this country.
There has been no reference to the serious housing crisis in Canada. We have heard about the minister's task force and we are looking forward to being in Newfoundland when it arrives there. There has been no reference to what this government intends to do about the thousands of Canadians who, because of rising interest rates, are deprived of their rights under the National Housing Act, and the effect on those in lower income brackets.
In my city our people suffer from a lack of adequate housing and from a lack of adequate subsidized housing, and a means to buy such accommodation. Yet no reference is made to housing in the speech from the throne. This is a very serious problem which affects all Canadians but which adversely affects certain areas in Canada more than others. When the people of the maritime provinces suffer because of the inadequacies of a particular federal program it means a real hardship to the people of Newfoundland, a hardship which they are expected to bear, and bear silently.
The people of Newfoundland want justice and want to be treated like other Canadians. If a just society means the end of programs which mean so much to Atlantic Canada and particularly to Newfoundland then we want no more of it. We have lived through the war on poverty but we still have poverty in abundance. We have people who still suffer because of the highest per capita cost of living ever, and the lowest per capita income in all of Canada. Hon. members do not know what poverty is and the Prime Minister does not know what poverty is, but his colleague from Newfoundland knows about it. He has seen it on the south coast of his constituency. My colleagues from Newfoundland know what poverty is; they have seen it in every bay and inlet in the province. My colleagues from New Brunswick know what it is; they have seen it in the northern part of that province. Poverty is a real thing, not something you can legislate by trite phrases. It is
September 17, 1968	COMMONS
something that has to be tackled with concrete programs.
One of the real inadequacies of our federal system results from the fact that the implementation of national programs does not give due regard to the peculiar and special economic circumstances of the different regions of the country. The National Housing Act, as it now exists, is fine for the people of urban Ontario, but for the people of Newfoundland and certain other parts of the maritime provinces it means they must be content to remain outside the pale; they must be content to keep their large families in substandard housing and to go without the things they see others having in abundance.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
We want justice. If there is to be a just society, we want to take part in it. We want to see an end to the pork-barrel system of politics that we in the province of Newfoundland have suffered from for 20 years, and which we now see evidenced as the first and only step this government seems able to take with any degree of assuredness.
We want to participate in the Canadian life. Our people want adequate housing. They want a fair return for their labours. They want jobs. They do not want to suffer the morally crippling effects of welfare. They want to be able to hold up their heads and earn an honest living like other citizens of Canada. I am sure my colleagues from Newfoundland, as they talk about the fisheries crisis which we have, as they talk about the failure of the Liberal government to live up to its promise to implement the 12-mile fishing limit of 1963, as they talk of hardships imposed upon our people because of the National Housing Act as it is now constituted, will re-echo my words. They will re-echo my words when they talk with feeling and experience of the real poverty that exists in this country and the crippling effects of this poverty, on the young especially. They will say, as I say now, that if there is to be a just society, let it come quickly because we want to be a part of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I am pleased to join with those who spoke before me to congratulate you for the trust put in you by parliament, a trust which, everyone agrees, you deserve to the highest degree. All hon. members can testify to that in this house.
DEBATES	135
The Address-Mr. LeBlanc
I wish also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Corbin and Mar-chand). It is interesting to note the particular characteristics of those two young members.
The first one, the hon. member for Mada-waska-Victoria, symbolises for us that race of hardy pioneers, the Acadians. In hardship as in the struggle for survival, they always showed tenacity, courage, pride and efficiency and that is an example for all the citizens of our great country.
The second one, member of the great Amerindian family, represents a proud group also, a group which only asks to be allowed to live and progress on the vast territory of Canada. Both, their presence and their influence, make us understand the prodigious mosaic of the peoples who work together towards the development and improvement of our country.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the great hopes set by the Canadian people as a whole on the new team, the new cabinet which now governs our country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) especially deserves the admiration of the Canadian community. We believe he is one of the most cultured Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to address myself to you once again. I am proud to represent again, in this house, my constituents of Rimouski.
During these last few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I intend first to express to you my humble feelings about the contents of the Speech from the Throne and to deal briefly with a few problems of rather regional concern but also, in actual fact, interregional in scope.
We all remember the platform outlined by the Liberal party during the last election. Based on the fundamental principle of a just society, that platform indicated the measures to be taken in order to achieve four basic objectives: the Canadian unity, the just society, a booming economy and the efficient and reasonable role of Canada in the world.
A perusal of the Speech from the Throne shows us that the government, at the very start of its term, applies faithfully its platform which is for us a source of satisfaction. I know that our colleagues in the opposition behave like disappointed men.
We know that the Canadian people want action, efficiency, results and that the efficiency is always evidenced by tangible results. To act, a program is necessary, planning is
136	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. LeBlanc required. The Speech from the Throne is a program, it is a supplement to the platform of the Liberal party, of the government.
The Speech from the Throne deals with problems which will be the object of our efforts in order to find solutions. We do not doubt that this session, which is at its very beginning, will see at work an active and dynamic government. The projects which the present government intends to present and put into effect during the session will certainly continue to take shape. It must be admitted that the government takes care not to make nice promises, merely election promises, to the Canadian people.
The Speech from the Throne, in our view, truly reflects the principles and statements made by the right hon. Prime Minister during the last election. Drawn up in a spirit of restraint, it takes into account in a constructive, objective and practical way, the social and economic problems of our country. We must first be pleased by the fact that it provides for the improvement and modernization of parliamentary procedure and this will allow the hon. members-the representatives of the people-to discuss freely but rationally the legislation introduced during the last session.
For example, during the last session, several bills remained outstanding because of the chronic slowness with which the house dispatches its business. It is easy to understand why the present government must bring up again some of its bills which are important and assential to the evolution of the country.
Moreover, one can only congratulate the government on undertaking, after dealing with these essential matters, its program intended to provide the conditions necessary for the materialization of the just society of which the Prime Minister has spoken so much, and rightly. It is also not only normal but necessary that the government, having considered all aspects of the building of a just society, should establish a priority list before setting to work. Hon. members have already seen that one of the priority items is the unity of the country, and that constitutional reforms will naturally have to be suggested in order to ensure this unity. Whatever some people may say, it is clear that the government will continue to intensify the war against poverty by asking for close co-operation at all levels of government. We can therefore hope to see a greater co-ordination which will ensure the implementation of the measures taken in this respect.

We all recognize that a great step forward was taken lately as far as respect for the languages of our two main ethnical groups is concerned. The government has announced that measures will be taken in order to make sure that every citizen will be able to use his own language when dealing with any federal government agency or service.
The Speech from the Throne also refers to problems affecting Canadians in their private life, as for example regional disparities and urban development. The Economic Council of Canada recently advised that the social policy of the government should be entirely reexamined. Both regional disparities and war against poverty are, among other problems, very complex matters, as shown by world history.
It is therefore normal for the government to proceed with caution instead of resorting to hasty solutions, and we understand that. Each component of the Speech from the Throne is a reminder of the over-all picture suggested by the Prime Minister during the last election. Not only is he urging government members to action but also, it seems to me, opposition members.
Along with the majority of people who voted for this, we welcome the Speech from the Throne heartfully and we anticipate at the beginning of this session an era of dynamic evolution for the Canadian people who are proud to follow such a leader as the right hon. Prime Minister. Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would be greatly interested, as I mentioned at the beginning, in touching on a few regional problems, bearing in mind inter-regional interests which are part of the Canadian policy.
I am particularly interested in the regional development policy of this government, as I was in that of the previous governments, because everyone knows that the constituency of Rimouski is part of the lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe regions which have been labelled as a "pilot territory".
During the election campaign, I had the opportunity to mention different facts and ideas about these regional development projects in our region. I did not mention the name or the title ARDA; neither did I mention the title BAEQ (Eastern Quebec Development Board). The reason for this is that I was under the impression those names or designations had become somewhat taboo among people in general. People in our region, as every Canadian knows, are eager for results. They
September 17, 1968

are industrious people, people who want some action. That is why we are sometimes inclined to forget that surveys are necessary. It is obvious, however, that they must not last too long.
That is why, during the election campaign,
I limited myself to speaking about our five-year program. Instead of speaking of planning, I merely spoke of our five-year program while thinking of the government program administered by our Liberal party. Like all the members, I was not ashamed to speak about it as our program, because out of $260 million to be spent in the implementation of this five-year program, $212 million will be paid out by the federal government. We had the pleasure, towards the end of April, of welcoming the present Prime Minister of Canada who came to our riding to preside over the historical signing of the agreement the premier of Quebec on behalf of the provincial government, and by the then Minister of Forestry and Rural Development for the federal government.
The program which will be implemented as the result of this agreement, interests us to the highest degree. That is why the people back home live in hope and look with confidence towards the Ottawa government.
This program is divided into eight points. To sum it up quickly, it is related first to the development, the reorganization of agriculture in our area. It also relates to the rational redevelopment of our forests as a whole, our fishing industries and to the tourist industry. It also concerns the review of wages paid to manpower in urban development, in transport, which are of prime importance in this part of Canada. This program should also provide an incentive for scientific research which is of the highest importance for the economic development of an area or a country.
Our people are mostly concerned with the role played by Ottawa, by the government of Canada, in the implementation of this program.
In view of the responsibility that the federal government assumed when it decided to spend $212 million for the implementation of that program and the rational redevelopment of our region, we all know that it is of the utmost importance that the federal government should exercise very close and adequate supervision.
It is obvious that, on account of our constitution, the implementation of that program is first of all the concern of ARDA-Quebec. But,

The Address-Mr. LeBlanc on the other hand, everyone agrees that the part played by the provincial officials in the implementation of those objectives should be supervised, not because we lack confidence in them, their work, their research and their realizations but because we fear that their scientific or intellectual or theoretical interest in the study of those projects might lead them to forget that we expect results as quickly as possible. That is the area where our people hope that the federal government, with the Prime Minister of Canada, will play a prominent part.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
One aspect of this program in particular attracts our attention, the problem of farmers. Because of the movement of rural people towards the cities-which seems to be at a point of no return,-a movement which is not particular to Canada but is worldwide-our farmers are very anxious and wonder how they will be able to earn a reasonable enough yearly income with the present evolution of our social and economic order.
I would like to draw the attention of the house and the government on two points in particular. Our farmers are specializing in the dairy industry. They have problems of quotas about which we heard so often in recent years. This quota policy is improving every day thanks to the interest taken in that matter by our governments and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). On the other hand, since the lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe area, which is anxious to live in keeping with the Canadian development, has been selected, as I said earlier, as a special development area, the farmers would like the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the Canadian Dairy Commission, to pay a special attention to the allocation of quotas in their area.
If, because of the present legislative structures concerning those quotas, it is impossible to prevent, so to speak, the abandoned quotas from leaving the area, would it not be possible to take a special measure so that the farmer of a pilot area may get an additional quota, so that he too could play his own part in the rationalization of our own dairy industry, our farmers' specialty.
In the program implementing the federal-provincial agreement which followed the report submitted by the Eastern Quebec Development Board, there is a point concerning cattle breeding. In our area, we are not trying to compete madly with anyone; we simply want to keep what we have and to develop it. It would seem that, in our areas, a certain specialization might be developed, even if not on a very large scale, at least on a
138	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. George Muir reasonable scale, and cattle breeding would be that specialization.
For two years, we have been taking steps to develop and promote that business at home that new farm industry, if one may put it so. We encountered many difficulties. In conjunction with the further steps that I shall certainly take in favour of our people at home, I ask in particular the Minister of Agriculture to pay special attention to that problem in order to help us solve it and encourage our farmers to practise breeding rationally, for the good of our area and in the interest of interregional co-operation for which our country is renowned.
Before concluding my remarks, I wish to emphasize the problem of transportation. The district where we live is located in the eastern part of the province of Quebec, and we have air and sea transportation.
Back home, air transportation is operated by a private company. In accordance with the policy and the philosophy of the responsible members in this house which encourages private enterprise, co-operation should exist between private enterprise and government agencies. It seems to us that federal agencies which are also carrying out studies on transportation should give a special attention to private transportation in the province of Quebec, especially in our region. The Crown corporation which ensures transportation in our country is the pride of all Canadians. But we cannot understand that this air company should sometimes enter into very close competition with certain private and responsible companies working for the rational development of our country.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for having given me once more the opportunity of speaking in this house. I believe that when reading over the last Speech from the Throne, in the light of the small problems I have just raised and for which we hope a solution will be found as soon as possible, the people of our areas, particularly those of my own district, will be proud to belong to Canada. I feel confident that this difficult problem of regional disparities so often referred to in the Speech from the Throne will gradually disappear. Within a few months, we shall all find that our efforts and our work will have brought results and we shall be even more proud to live in Canada in unity, justice and prosperity.

speechtext:
For too long the Liberal party has simply refused to admit that an agricultural community exists in Canada. That party has consistently written that community off. They have ignored it. For the past five years they have been content to advance only a token agricultural policy. During the election campaign the Prime Minister pronounced a Liberal agricultural policy. The best that can be said for it is that at least that is something the former leader of the party and the former minister did not achieve. It will be interesting to see whether the policy that was enunciated on the hustings will be carried into government policy. The Pearson government solved the problems of agriculture in its own way: It had no policy. Let us hope that the present administration will not be that short-sighted or arrogant.
Since 1963, I am afraid, the Canadian farmer has become the forgotten man, the expendable man. This I believe is a result of deliberate and calculated Liberal policy, based on the fact that a larger harvest of votes is to be garnered in the urban areas and that larger financial contributions may be expected from eastern industry.
There are, however, one or two points about the Canadian farming community that the Prime Minister and his government will do well to bear in mind. Agriculture earns $1 out of every $8 that is earned by Canadian trade. On the basis of 1965 figures, the latest available, farmers pay about $1 of every $10 paid in income taxes. Disregarding taxes and personal savings, the agricultural community has more than $1.5 billion to spend annually. It spends that money roughly in the proportion of 50 per cent on services, 40 per cent on non-durable goods and 10 per cent on durable goods. These facts surely are of some importance to the rest of Canada.
While it may be true that the farm population and the number of farms have been cut in half over the past 35 years, the actual number of acres devoted to agriculture has increased substantially. The value of all Canadian agricultural products in 1966 approached $3.5 billion. The total capital value of Canadian farms in 1966 was close to $20 billion. Farming, the industry of agriculture, has certainly changed, but only in nature and not in importance. I hope this government will bear some of these facts in mind, since the speech from the throne reflected only a dim awareness of them.
The Address-Mr. George Muir
In the speech I noted with particular interest the sentence concluding with the words: -intends to investigate immediately a number of methods for promoting greater efficiency in the production and marketing of grains, including the establishment of a national grains council.
I shall deal with the first part of that statement later. At the moment the latter part is of concern to me. In the past Liberal governments have been strong for establishing bodies with high sounding titles and sweeping terms of reference. Unfortunately, once set up those bodies have largely been ignored by the government, particularly when the advice of such bodies or their recommendations happened to be at odds with the party political interests of the moment.
The setting up of a national grains council is a most commendable step. Such a body could be of great assistance to the grain industry and the Canadian economy as a whole, provided it is not used as a niche in which to hide Liberal bagmen or defeated candidates. The grain council will be of little use to anyone if its setting up is mere window dressing, if its recommendations are sidetracked and ignored by the Liberal government, or treated lightly, as have so consistently the reports of the Economic Council of Canada over the past five years.
Another interesting part of the speech from the throne was that part dealing with plans to set up national marketing boards to deal with various types of agricultural produce. This part of the speech has a brave and progressive though not new ring. The carefully chosen wording reveals nothing of the constitutional hurdles and other problems that make the establishment of such boards difficult and long drawn out affairs.
The speech also mentions widening the credit term for farmers, increasing payments for farm stored grain, as well as other measures. In their way all these are necessary and admirable. At best they are palliatives, not cures; stop-gap measures, not lasting remedies. The Canadian agricultural community needs more from this government than gestures and token actions. It needs the assurance of the government's genuine and continuing concern. It wants full recognition and fair treatment. Surely one small corner must have been set aside for agriculture in the great, new just society.
On his inspection tour of Manitoba's sodden grain fields, the new Minister of Agriculture saw no immediate crisis. Actually, the crisis in those agricultural areas began last winter
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. George Muir from government action as from government apathy. It is a comparatively new industry and one that is vital to my riding of Lisgar. The oil seed industry has been hard hit in recent months by the free flow of cheaper foreign material into Canada. I am one who feels the Canadian farmer was sacrificed to industry in the recent Kennedy round negotiations at Geneva, and was used to buy preference for manufacturing in the agreement subsequently signed by our government. Consider only the plight of the oil seed growers I am talking about.
On September 3 the Altona, Manitoba, crushing plant told its sunflower seed growers that the price of sunflower seed oil had not improved since last May, that it had remained at about nine cents per pound as compared with the average price of about 14J cents over the last ten years. The blame for this condition was placed squarely on the cheap free flow of sunflower seed oil into Canada from eastern European growers, mainly the U.S.S.R. and its satellites.
The report stated that a brief, which was supported by many seed crushing plants and by the rapeseed Growers Association, sent to the federal government had offered the full co-operation of the vegetable oil industry in working out the pressing problems of the industry. To quote the report:
To my knowledge the Industry has received no response from the government as to their intentions regarding our requests.
Here again is glaring proof of the government's indifference to the problems plaguing various sectors of the agricultural industry.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct the attention of the house to a question of particular importance to my area, although I believe it to be equally important to the province of Manitoba and to the country as a whole. I mention it because I received a faint glimmer of hope from the reference in the speech from the throne to the government's concern about the threat of growing pollution of our water supplies.
The question I refer to is known as the Pembina river basin development. It is an imaginative, necessary and quite practical plan to ensure industrial and agricultural expansion, and economic prosperity for a large tract of land both within Canada and across the border in the United States. The Pembina river system lies in the extreme south of Manitoba and includes territory across the border in North Dakota. For this reason, when the idea was first advanced it

was passed as a reference to the International Joint Commission for an opinion. That was done back in 1962. By 1965 public hearings were held in the area by the International Joint Commission, and on October 6, 1967 that body reported favourably upon the development scheme to the Canadian and United States governments.
To Manitoba, as to any other region, water is vital. It becomes more so as the population increases, and as industrial and agricultural development increases. Manitoba is abundantly supplied with water, but unfortunately a great deal of the supply is in the more remote and inaccessible northern part. This makes the control and conservation of water available in other regions, particularly in the south, a matter of utmost urgency. This is even more urgent when those areas are the ones containing the maximum population, and industrial and agricultural potential. Such an area is the Pembina river district.
The great problem, one that increases as development increases, is that the natural supply varies widely in rate and volume with the seasons, and over a cycle of years. Left in its natural state the water supply of southern Manitoba varies from over abundance in the spring to near drought in fall and winter. Over a period of years the area may experience, unpredictably, abnormal supplies of water or practically none at all.
This makes it essential to take steps to ensure a steadier, more reliable year-round supply, year in and year out, from our natural water resources. As with all resources, the key is control and conservation. It is no exaggeration to say that water is the life blood of this important segment of the Canadian economy. Without it agriculture might struggle along on a hit or miss basis. No industry would be developed. The population would progressively dwindle as young men and women were driven elsewhere in search of work, and what could be a rich, flourishing and valuable part of the Canadian economy and of Canada's social fabric would be lost.
When the matter was referred to the International Joint Commission it was asked to look into and recommend on three points, domestic water supply and sanitation, control of floods, and irrigation. In the spring of 1965 the commission reported that they had three plans that were "practicable, economically feasible and of mutual advantage to both countries." These plans were found to be sound on the basis of the three main points
September 17, 1968

that the commission had been asked to consider, supply and sanitation, flood control, and irrigation.
Maurice Western, in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 15, 1965, wrote in part:
The most urgent needs of the lower basin are protection from floods and, paradoxically, the provision of an adequate water supply for urban, industrial and agricultural purposes.
The International Joint Commission study, on which public hearings were held in June, 1965 said in one passage:
If conditions are left as they are, the population of the basin can be expected to continue to gradually decrease ... lack of dependable water supplies has retarded both industrial and urban growth.
I have used these quotations to emphasize a point because it is the most important point about this development, one that has entirely escaped the minister responsible in the federal government, or perhaps been deliberately avoided by him. The point is that the Pembina development is not primarily designed as an irrigation measure or as a measure to help agriculture alone. It is a measure to stimulate industrial and social development for a very large area, an area whose potential could only bring great benefits far beyond its own region and even far beyond the province.
The complaint of the people of the region, and my chief complaint today, is that this project, already studied exhaustively, and approved by a body representing two national governments, has been callously pigeonholed by a new minister without even the courtesy of a full explanation. In Winnipeg recently the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) dismissed the whole Pembina river development as "a low priority" plan whose chief value lay purely in its role as an irrigation work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to join with those who have preceded me in extending to you, sir, something more than merely a perfunctory congratulation on your re-election to the high office as Speaker of this house. During my comparatively short experience here I have come to appreciate the dignity, the capacity and the ability with which you have discharged the duties of your very high office. At the same time I wish to extend to Mr. Deputy Speaker my congratulations on his appointment, and to wish him well. He is comparatively young in office and I am confident that he will improve with age. I think we can expect also that he will preside over the proceedings of this assembly with dignity.
I should like also to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both gentlemen have discharged with eloquence the role assigned them in this traditional debate. This speaks well of their ability to perform the duties they will be called upon to perform as members of the house.
In the relatively short time at my disposal as succinctly and as clearly as I can I should like to place before the government and before the house the economic conditions of the Atlantic area today, and of course with particular reference to the economic conditions as we find them in my province. I do this in the hope that the government will act just as quickly as is humanly possible to correct the regional disparity which now exists between this area and the rest of Canada.
We in the Atlantic provinces of course wish to make the fullest possible contribution to Canada's development, but we also want to participate in that development. As the Economic Council of Canada so very correctly pointed out just a short time ago, the ultimate purpose of our economic and social goals must be to provide all Canadians with access to a higher material standard of living and a higher quality of life. That is the recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada.
Therefore I say it is most important to recognize that if all Canadians are to share in higher living standards there must be a strong and stable over-all growth. Nothing else will satisfy. In the past six or seven years
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. McQuaid
there has been a sustained economic growth in Canada as a whole. I believe it can be correctly stated that the economy of Canada has been expanding over the last five or six years without too many reversals. But that has not been the case in the Atlantic provinces.
I should like to take this opportunity to place on the record some very tangible proof that our economy is not expanding in ratio with the expansion taking place all across this country. First of all, if we look at total personal income, we find that in Canada as a whole between the years 1961 and 1966 personal income increased by 50.3 per cent. That is an increase of 50.3 per cent in Canada as a whole. In the Atlantic region however this increase was only 42.7 per cent, almost 8 per cent less than the national average.
In 1966 the personal income in the Atlantic provinces averaged only $1,480. What was the Canadian average? It was $2,134. In other words, the average personal income in the Atlantic region during that period has been only 69.4 per cent of the Canadian average. I am sure all hon. members of this house will recognize that this is not as it should be.
Perhaps before I begin to become too involved in figures I might be permitted to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was attempting to point out the economic disparity which exists between the Atlantic provinces and the other areas of Canada. As proof of this disparity I mentioned the difference between the per capita income in the Atlantic area and the rest of Canada. Let me suggest as a very clear example of this that in my own province of Prince Edward Island the average per capita income is only $1,382. That is the second lowest of any province in Canada, and this is only 64.8 per cent of the national average.
Let us look at the unemployment which exists in the Atlantic area as compared with the rest of Canada. Our unemployment rate of 7.9 per cent continues to be excessively high, when compared with the 5.3 per cent in Canada as a whole. This is the situation in spite of one of the greatest periods of expansion in Canadian history. As evidence that

our unemployment rate continues to remain unacceptably high, I would point to the fact that in 1965, for example, the unemployment insurance commission paid $52,500,000 in unemployment insurance claims in the Atlantic provinces. Our rate of population growth is also very far behind that of the rest of Canada. Between 1961 and 1966 the population of the Atlantic provinces increased by only 0.8 per cent per year compared with almost 2 per cent per year for Canada as a whole.
Migration from the area has been a major factor in this small regional increase. This migration comes as no surprise, when we consider the per capita income gap between our region and Canada as a whole. When one considers that large gap, there is naturally a tendency to move from the Atlantic provinces in search of better opportunities elsewhere. The maritime provinces have been losing population since before confederation. Since 1881, with the exception of one ten year period between 1931 and 1941, migration has never been less than 75,000 people every ten years. Since 1961 we have been losing more than 20,000 people per year. If this present trend continues we will have lost about 200,000 people between 1961 and 1971.
Migration on this scale must be examined very carefully, because if it continues at this present high rate we may very well have less than the labour force required to produce the goods and services necessary to provide a level of income sufficient to prevent a widening of the present income gap between our people and those in the rest of Canada.
This trend has left us with a comparatively small number of people in what we like to call the productive age group, that group between 18 and 64 years of age. They are the ones who are most likely to be in the labour force and they, of course, are the ones that are most likely to leave when the income is not sufficient to sustain them. About 30 per cent of our total population falls within the less than 15 year age group, and 55 per cent falls within the productive age group, as compared to the Canadian average of 58 per cent.
I think this situation was pointed out very well some years ago in a report known as the Economic History of the Atlantic provinces, from which I should like to quote:
For years, the movement of population has been out of rather than into the maritime provinces with the result that the population is heavily weighted on the side of the very old and the very young, leaving the number in the now productive age
September 17, 1968

group relatively lower than in other parts of the Dominion; and this, in itself, other things being equal, lowers the average income.
There is one more important implication to this problem of migration so far as the government is concerned. If the number of taxpayers in proportion to the population is relatively low, and it is on this basis that we in the Atlantic area legitimately agree that we are entitled to more help from the central government here in Ottawa, not by way of handouts and not necessarily by the transfer of income to our region but rather through the generation of income within the area. That is what we want, something that will generate income within this area.
I am not particularly knowledgeable about the financial condition of the provinces in the Atlantic region, other than my own, but I do know about the situation in Prince Edward Island. I should like at this time to place on the record some figures which will indicate the serious financial position in which the province of Prince Edward Island finds itself today. We have a population of only 110,000 people, with a per capita income which is the second lowest of any province in Canada. Naturally, therefore, with such a low per capita income our people are not able to contribute to the treasury by way of taxes to the same extent as people living in other provinces in Canada who have higher incomes. However, as citizens of Canada we are entitled to enjoy the same essential services enjoyed by people living in other provinces.
Our provincial government is doing its best to provide these services, but in attempting to do so it has brought the province almost to the brink of bankruptcy. On March 31, 1968 the net debt of the province was $64,490,000, and it is estimated that by March 31, 1969 this debt will be $65,506,000. This is a per capita debt of $595, the highest per capita debt of any province in Canada. This is a province which is not rich in natural resources but is dependant almost entirely on two primary industries, fishing and farming.
In addition to that net debt of $65,506,000 the government has contingency liabilities of $15,500,000 making a total of $81 million or a per capita debt of almost $737. Debt charges alone and this will give an idea of how serious the situation is-amount to $7,817,000 or almost $22,000 per day.
Do hon. members know how much in taxes the taxpayers of Prince Edward Island are able to contribute to the treasury. One member of the provincial government suggested

The Address-Mr. McQuaid the other day that the saturation point had been reached. This year we will collect through taxes only $14,788,000. It is going to cost $7,800,000 just to pay the interest on what we owe. How are we possibly going to finance the departments of government? This is only a small province, but education alone requires an expenditure of $12 million, health services require the expenditure of $9 million and highway maintenance, capital and other expenditures amount to $9 million. This is only some of the money we must have in order to provide our people, as citizens af this country, with the essential services to which they are entitled.
Something must be done to close this economic gap which now exists between the Atlantic area and other parts of Canada. Some action must be taken by this government immediately. I would make one suggestion as to how we might help close this gap, and to do so would be of tremendous assistance to the province of Prince Edward Island. The government should immediately commence construction of the Northumberland strait crossing. This is something that has been definitely promised to us by the Liberal government, but at the present time there seems to be some uncertainty as to whether the government intends to go ahead with the project. There seems to be something hollow about the statement that the project is to go ahead, something disquieting about the mumblings that there will be delays in starting the project. Let me remind hon. members that this causeway is not a gift to Prince Edward Island. Our gap in communications compared with the rest of Canada needs to be effectively closed, as guaranteed by our entry into confederation.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
In 1965, very shortly before the last general election, the then prime minister announced that the causeway would be built. I quote from a newspaper report of July 8, 1965:
Prime Minister Pearson announced today that tenders will be called later this year for a combined tunnel, bridge and causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Construction is expected to start next April, and Mr. Pearson said at a press conference he hopes it will be completed in late 1970.
That, I suggest, is a definite commitment by the government to go ahead with this project. They immediately sent the then minister of mines, Mr. MacNaught, to New Brunswick, put a hard hat on him, put him on a bulldozer and he turned the first sod. However, Mr. September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. McQuaid Speaker, I suggest that he drove the bulldozer too fast, because he turned the first sod that day, and perhaps the last.
Then an election was drawing closer and the government decided they would definitely convince the people of Prince Edward Island that the causeway would be built. They sent to the island a man who was at that time the champion of Prince Edward Island, the man tagged as the best friend the island ever had, the then minister of transport, Mr. Pickers-gill. Hon. members will remember him. When he was in opposition he was up and down in his seat like a jack-in-the-box, popping questions to the government as to when they would start construction of the causeway. Perpendicular Jack; he was up more than down. He told the people of the island that the causeway would be started. He said, "My heart bleeds for the people of Prince Edward Island." Wasn't that sad. The poor old fellow must have bled to death, because there was an election that year, the Liberals returned no members from Prince Edward Island and we heard no more from him afterwards.
Then they sent over the then secretary of state for external affairs. I suggest that he made history when he came to the province, because for the first time in a long political career he really gave an answer to a question. Somebody asked him if the government were really going to build the causeway, and he said yes, the causeway would be built. Then we had the election. No Liberal members were returned from Prince Edward Island in the 1965 election, and the causeway was apparently forgotten until we again came close to an election. I have here some statements that I should like to place on the record. I think these statements should convince the members of the government that each and every one of them is committed to the construction of this project.
On October 5, 1967, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) said:
The strait crossing will become a reality because the Ottawa government is committed to it.
What more concrete statement than that do you want? The then minister of finance, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) said on July 12, 1967:
What surprises me more than anything is the fact that so many islanders seem to feel that the Northumberland strait crossing will never be built.
He gave the reassurance that the crossing not only would be built but, in his own words, would be built in accordance with the
(Mr. McQuaid.]
original schedule that was announced, namely that the crossing would be completed by not later than 1970. He told Prince Edward Islanders that face to face, right in their own province.
The then minister of public works said on May 31, 1967, as reported in Hansard at page 779:
I would lilce to conclude by reasserting the government's intention to continue with this project. I might add that the causeway approach road on Prince Edward Island will soon be completed, and tenders for construction of a highway interchange at Albany, P.E.I., are expected to be called this summer.
These, I suggest, are very definite commitments on the part of this government to proceed with this great project. Now we have the era of the new society, the just society. This was going to be "it" for sure. Surely now, with a just society, we would get a causeway. They took the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) over, they had a pipe band, the pipers played "Road to the Isles", the Grits cheered, and this was going to be "it"; there would be no delays and we would have the causeway. So far nothing has been done. I think the Prime Minister said this was going to be a jumping parliament. I have not seen much jumping yet.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset congratulate Your Honour on reappointment to your office. May I also offer my congratulations to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) on his new duties. I do not see him in his seat at the moment. I am sorry that my companion member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) is not present, because I very much wanted to say to him that I hope that, with me, he will be able to forward the business of Canada, which I am sure is the main purpose for our being here.
I think it is well that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) went to western Canada recently and looked at the situation which exists there, particularly in southern Manitoba and southern Saskatchewan where we were severely plagued by bad weather during the harvest season. As he quite properly noted, it would be a week or two before we can properly assess the situation. Weather has to take its course, and all of us sincerely hope that we will get the fine weather which is needed to enable these farmers to harvest their crops. As the minister observed, and as I did when I drove through that area, the ground was so wet at that time that one did not see much harvest machinery in operation. I am sure that if these conditions continue, the minister will come to the house with some recommendations on what might be undertaken. However, these are natural factors with which farmers must live. I am sure the minister has learned this during his lifetime, as indeed have I.
What we are concerned with here are the things we can do ourselves and which the government can do to improve farming conditions. We are concerned about the rate of unemployment in the cities and in the countryside; we are concerned about the levels of farm income and about the interest rates which farmers must pay for the loans they must have to continue their operation, just as also do the city dwellers to run their businesses and to build and maintain their houses. We are concerned about grain sales and about prices which affect not only the farmers but also the city dwellers. In short, what we are concerned about is the ability of the individual to survive in the economic jungle of this
The Address-Mr. Gleave society and to make a place for himself and a living for his family. It is well that the government is also concerned about it, as was made evident in the following statement from the throne speech;
My government is deeply concerned to provide and to ensure increased justice, dignity and recognition to the individual, particularly in an age which is characterized by large governments, industrial automation, social regimentation and old-fashioned laws.
I do not know much about old fashioned laws. It seems to me that most of them are old fashioned, because we live in a society which is governed by common law developed through the centuries. However, if we can protect the rights of the individual and if we can enhance the living standards and the quality of life of the individual, this is what we should do. I doubt we can do it, however, by cancelling the winter works program. Very shortly after my election, and before coming to Ottawa for this session I received a number of resolutions from the city of Saskatoon, roughly half of which is in my constituency, and the town of Biggar, which is a small town serving the C.N.R. and the farmers in the surrounding areas. Both of these communities asked that the winter works program be continued and that it be carefully discussed.
As a result of one of those wires, I sought and had a meeting with the mayor of Saskatoon because frankly I felt I needed more information. He explained to me the benefits of the winter works program, especially in relieving unemployment, and the way in which the city and the surrounding communities were able effectively to use it. Very shortly thereafter and before this parliament met-and this may or may not have been significant-the winter works program was cancelled. In the coming winter we will feel the effect of that decision in the communities I mentioned. These communities are carrying a heavy load. The potash industry around Saskatoon is steadily developing, and as it employs a greater number of men it will throw a greater load on the surrounding communities on which it depends for services and for housing for the people who work in that industry. In effect, the city and towns such as Vanscoy, Delisle and Asquith have become the dormitories of the potash industry. These communities must house the people, must educate their children and must provide all the amenities of living required by a fast growing community.
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. Gleave
Saskatoon is faced with the installation of a $6 million sewage system to control pollution and to dispose of the wastes of a great city. It seems to me that under these circumstances the government should be moving forward, not backward, in helping such urban communities. As is described by the Economic Council of Canada, these communities must also take care of the manpower surplus which comes from the farms. People are moving away from farms and are swelling our urban centres.
In the last year or 18 months we have been faced with rapidly increasing interest rates which have not only affected the cities and small communities but also our farms. As a result, in the last eight months or so farmers have simply not been able to get farm improvement loans. These loans are essential to the well-being of our farmers because this is the method they have used for keeping and maintaining adequate machinery on their farms. Without such a loans program, farmers will not be able to keep the kind and the number of machines they need to run their farms efficiently. I know because I tried it myself.
Farmers who have gone to banks asking for farm improvement loans have been refused them. They have been told they could have all the money they wanted but had to pay the current interest rate, which may be as high as 71 or 8 per cent. We were told in the throne speech that some provision will be made to alleviate the situation. However, I hope that as a result of such a provision the interest rates will not be raised and that we will continue the same stable interest rates on farm improvement loans which will enable us to obtain the money we need for farming. The Economic Council of Canada has said that it is essential to expand the farming community by increasing efficiency in production. One of the things which will be needed is easily available capital at rates which the community can afford.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
From the information I have received, in a good many instances the story connected with the Farm Credit Corporation is not much better in respect of the amount of money lent than is the case with farm improvement loans. I have received a letter from a farmer in west central Saskatchewan whose son wanted to buy a quarter section of land. He said he approached the Farm Credit Corporation and was told he would have to mortgage two sections of land, including the home
[Mr. Gleave.l

quarter and buildings, and as well agree that the son would have use of a complete line of machinery at no cost to him. This man suggested that instead of such a drastic step he would allow the corporation to hold title to one half section, but the offer was flatly refused. As a result a land company, with finances from outside the provinces, bought the land. I am using this man's experience only to illustrate the situation. He stated that this is a common occurrence throughout the prairies. Here a man is asked, in order that his son may buy a quarter section, to mortgage eight quarter sections or put under mortgage the total land assets he has acquired in probably a lifetime of work.
This man's experience is typical of the assistance we are offering farmers. I suggest that if this sort of policy is continued we will fall far short of the increased productivity and efficiency about which the economic council is talking. It is the practice, and it is the tradition of our farm lending agencies to serve the farmer, not to exploit him. When security of this type is sought, it falls little short of exploitation. I hope that when these policies are reviewed we will correct this sort of thing and that we will maintain a stable interest rate. If necessary, I hope we will subsidize the rate of interest.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that there must be priorities. Well, all of us who are mature know that there are always priorities. We live with them every day of our lives on the farm. We paint the house or we buy another machine. We make a choice. In this society, we are going to have to make a choice. If we are going to have enough houses in the city of Saskatoon, and if we are going to have enough machinery on these farms, we shall have to maintain an interest rate that will make these things possible.
The Economic Council of Canada suggests that in the last decade the prices of farm products have increased much less than the prices of other products. I quote from its report:
With slow growth in demand for farm products, prices of farm products have increased much less than prices of other goods and services over the past two decades. This has meant that the prices of the goods sold by farmers have, on the average, increased less rapidly than the prices of goods purchased by farmers. And this has meant, in turn, that part of the income generating benefits arising from the rapid rate of growth of agricultural productivity have been shifted from the farm sector to other sectors of the economy.
The short term for that situation is the cost-price squeeze. We have been living with
Sepiember 17, 1968

it for a long time in the farming community. The situation has to be corrected by applying price supports and by giving other advantages to the farm sector if we are going to have a healthy agricultural economy. There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to continue with the volume of wheat sales we have and the prices we have had in the last year, we will be in serious economic difficulties in western Canada.
This morning one speaker said that farm machinery sales had dropped 30 per cent in one province. This is the first sign of difficulty. This chapter in the report of the Economic Council of Canada from which I have been quoting also focuses on the need for increased research in agriculture. The economic council believes this to be a matter of great importance. It says that the amount of research conducted, especially in the field of cereal grain, has lagged far behind. Certainly, it has. The last time I checked we had one full-time man doing wheat research in the province of Saskatchewan. We put "the wheat province" on our licence plates, but we devote the time of only one man to the task of getting the best varieties that can be grown in our province. As I said, if we are going to measure up in this field, then we have to increase our wheat sales. I note the government has committed itself to wheat sales amounting to 1.3 billion bushels in the next three years. This will be a little better than 400 million bushels of sales per year, >
which would be about 20 per cent less than the normal production.
If you really want to calculate some priorities, Mr. Speaker, try to calculate them if you are running a wheat farm on a six bushel quota. This really takes some priorities. I wanted to say something about the proposed national grain council. While I do not like to be overly critical about a program that is proposed, because I think we need all the programs we can get to assist us, I did check with two national farm organizations, the National Farmers Union and the head office of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Both of these organizations informed me they had not been consulted about the formation of such a council and had not yet received any invitation to join. I do not place too much emphasis on the fact that an invitation has not been received because the invitations may not yet have been sent out. However, I do consider it important that these organizations have not been consulted. It is almost a tradition by now in western Canada that when we
The Address-Mr. Gleave change our approach to wheat marketing or change the marketing structure, we do consult thoroughly with farm organizations. I think it is important. We face some pretty important decisions in western Canada in the field of grain.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The international grains agreement has come under fire or pressure. News reports have been telling us this ever since it was signed. Negotiations were no sooner completed in Geneva when price cutting began. The United States cut prices, and on that account we were in the doldrums all last winter. According to news reports we are still in the same position. Many people are advocating solutions. We are told by all kinds of people to do this, that or the other, whereas we really need a thorough examination of our entire position.
To date we have failed to use effectively the facilities which we have, such as the excellent laboratory facilities of the Board of Grain Commissioners. We could have used those jointly with the Canadian Wheat Board in an effective selling and promotional campaign such as our competitors make use of. We need a more effective staff overseas and we must know to a greater extent what our competitors and purchasers are doing.
Somebody out west told me that we have no agricultural attache in Moscow. I did not believe this until I came down here and checked into it. One would think that our government would take the step of appointing such an attache so that we might be informed adequately about the volume of grain production in Russia, about weather conditions, the varieties and qualities of grain being grown, and so on. The Wheat Board has two agencies overseas. I do not want to be too critical, Mr. Speaker, but we ought to have a more effective promotional and selling campaign overseas than we have.

We need a more effective research program. In its report the economic council tells us that we are spending in research far and away less than one of our competitors, the United States. I have talked to people in Saskatchewan, at the university and experimental station level, and I have found that the best way to describe our research program is

The Address-Mr. Fortin that it is just plainly inadequate. We should correct that situation.
I notice that a news report of September 12, I believe it was, said that grain industry men were to be called to a meeting to give the views of the grain industry. I hope that when those ministers responsible for the grain industry call the leaders of the industry to the meeting they will remember that the farmers are part of that grain industry. The farmer's interests and needs must be taken care of and his voice must be heard.
I conclude with a plea to this government to consider seriously the needs of the farmer and the predicament in which he finds himself. The farms of Canada have an immense productivity; but that productivity has not yet been fully developed. If our productivity is to be fully utilized and if our farm areas are to be fully developed then, surely it will be because it is worth while for people to stay in farming as a vocation and make it a way of life.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me today to be called upon to express before this historic house the thoughts, wishes, problems and aspirations of the 67,000 citizens of the riding of Lotbiniere, which is not necessarily behind the other ridings, even though, contrary to all the expert predictions, the majority of its people voted for the Ralliement Creditiste. The honour which has been given to me of speaking on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne is accompanied by the great joy of being able to sit by the side of a great man who has remained true to himself and who fights sincerely to defend convictions more important to him than any material comfort. I speak of the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.
