speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot begin this first short speech without greeting the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy chairman of Committees, who will, I am sure, show themselves to be most helpful and understanding towards a new member such as I.
Finally, I should like to greet all my new colleagues from all parties, to whom I extend my co-operation at any time for the advancement and welfare of our people and democratic institutions.
It is not easy to comment on a Speech from the Throne such as the one now before us, as


it compels us to go into deep thoughts the like of which are not found in it.
Mention was made, in the Speech from the Throne, of an elaborate legislation in terms of priorities already established. I should like to say, at this time, that the government should take into consideration the suggestions made by the opposition as regards the establishment of priorities. Otherwise, the situation would be very serious. For one thing, Parliament would lose its meaning. For another, if you consider carefully the Speech from the Throne, you soon realize that almost all the priorities stressed by this government are minor ones and relegate the individual to a place of minor importance.
We are told about 47 bills, but the main point does not lie there, and that is putting the Canadian dollar at the service of human beings. As long as money runs the world and crushes the individual, our society will reek with injustice, dishonesty, crime and despair to those who cannot rest at night without worrying about the next day. And there are hundreds of those people in each one of our ridings.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Since I have become a member of this new parliament, I have become acquainted with the reports of royal commissions of enquiry on banks, on government organization, on taxation, including those of the Economic Council of Canada and more specifically the last one.
If, on the one hand, one goes deeply into those reports, which are based on facts, on consultations, hearings and briefs and, on the other hand, one sees the inhuman means our fellow citizens resort to in order to survive and to live, as a young and new member, one could expect a positive Speech from the Throne, that would dig deep and invite the members of this house to tackle the roots of the real problems.
But what do we see?
We are invited in the Speech from the Throne to legislate on some 47 bills, most of them dealing with interests which are very limited geographically, socially and economically.
Of course the debate now going on can only be superficial-just like the speech itself by the way-since hon. members do not know what the various bills outlined in the Speech from the Throne contain or mean because everything is kept secret. That Speech from
September 17, 1968

the Throne reminds me of a man who wants to give his little family a proper home but whose hopes are soon thwarted because the monetary tool is either missing or too expensive; he must therefore be satisfied to dream and wait, which is what the government is doing. As I said a little earlier, we will be asked to consider 47 bills. But what good will they do? Will a governing principle preside over their drafting?
The Prime Minister, with his dream of a just society, will claim that they will be, but it is undeniable that his economic philosophy is based on conservatism, and not on progress and modernism.
At this point, I now refer to the Speech from the Throne where we can read:
We have taken and are taking effective strides toward economic conservation through progressively better use of our resources to achieve a high and long-term productivity.
By so doing, this government is advocating a doctrine of non participation in economic life.
There is a constant theme, a leitmotiv as it were, but this perfectly conceived refrain has a strange sound of status quo. And that is distressing.
I thought that a majority government would not be afraid of putting through reforms in depth and advocating a modern and progressive legislative philosophy.
I say this because as a Social Crediter I am convinced that the greatest problem in Canada is to connect fittingly three things: firstly, economic efficiency, secondly, social justice and thirdly, individual freedom.
Now, to achieve economic efficiency, social justice and individual freedom, the present financial institutions and others must be set at the pace of the human being and the community, because, in fact, institutions exist to serve those who want them, that is individuals. Let us not forget that unsuitable institutions, overtaken by technological development will certainly impair economic efficiency, in a context of social justice and individual freedom.
I would like the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to define his just society in unequivocal terms; I would like him to tell this house what he feels it is in reality in relation to people and things, within our Canadian society of 1968. I should like him to show me the exact relation he sees between the 47 bills he proposes and announces in the Speech from the Throne and his just society.
The Address-Mr. Fortin
In my opinion, the Speech from the Throne and the bills are one thing and the just society of the hon. Prime Minister is another.
We know full well, Mr. Speaker, that social and political conditions derive from and depend largely upon the economy. When the necessary economic controls are missing or blocked by inadequate or too conservative measures, any social, political or even constitutional legislation, becomes practically impracticable or inapplicable due to the restrictions imposed by the economy.
This is so true that the government recognizes it in the Speech from the Throne where it says:
In the complexities of modern society, the effective programs take time to develop and more time to implement. At all stages, they require financial and intellectual resources which are not unlimited and must be used with careful planning and the hard judgment of priorities.
Mr. Speaker, the economic, social, and political concepts are closely related and it is most urgent to restore our scale of values. We must give back to the individual the place which is rightly his, in other words we must put the economic concept and the results which follow to the service of the human being.
We must equip ourselves, as soon as possible, with the necessary economic controls so that we may, as administrators and legislators, fulfil our duties in an appropriate manner on the one hand and in conformity with the wishes of the people on the other hand.
Economic controls are a means and not an end, as is still believed by some of us in this house. They are tools provided to adjust, rectify, step up, restrain not the human being but the whole system or the national economic complex. The legislation submitted to us in the Speech from the Throne is silent about all those economic controls. It is rather obsolete, out-of-date, and inefficient. Frankly, I expected a modem, dynamic, balanced and mainly human legislation which would emphasize consumption and the consumer, in our automated world, and I confess that I am very disappointed.
Since in our modern economy machine takes on gradually the duties of man, the economy, directed by administrators and lawmakers, must be more and more man-oriented. In this field, the government must not shirk its prime and vital responsibilities for the welfare of the nation it administers.
For instance, the idea which gave birth to the Bank of Canada is now outmoded and
152	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fortin obsolete. In our system of overwhelming capitalism, where the rich get richer at the expense of the poor and where only big financiers can indulge in capitalization, the role of the Bank of Canada has become secondary and we even tend to wonder whether or not it still exists. Its duties are vague, its members are kept in the background, its administration is concealed, its achievements are unknown, and its links with the government of the Canadian nation are illusory.
Yet the Bank of Canada could be one of the most important levers of the economy if only the right decision was taken. But the governments which have followed one another for almost a hundred years have been unable to pull themselves together in order to make such a decision.
Politics must not be the art of making promises but rather the art of doing what is possible. What really matters is policies translated into facts. If the just society is to exist, it will have to be translated into facts, because people judge from facts.
I note that the Speech from the Throne lacks a philosophy of action looking towards the future.
The time for wishes is past; now is the time for determination and concrete action. Governments and parliamentarians should have taken, ages ago, the necessary steps to insure the defence and the promotion of consumers.
The problem of production and of productivity is solved once and for all. Considered in itself, our productivity is unlimited. We are on the wrong track, Mr. Speaker, if we believe the speech from the throne that suggests that the most serious economic problem in Canada is that of production. I declare here, in this house, that the major problem is related to the consumption of products and resources of our country and of other countries. The distribution of resources among consumers: this is the basic problem that is facing us and all Canadians expect us to come up with a fool-proof solution.
That is why several thousands of persons have voted for the Ralliement creditiste during the last election!
The Social credit did not die as some people predicted; it is very much alive and kicking, because people increasingly understand what the problem is.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Something one should never forget and which is at the root of this problem is the fact that income is not equitably apportioned out

DEBATES	September 17, 1968
among the producers, the distributors and the consumers once they are left on their own. The consumers are thus deprived of a large fraction of the assets they had secured in their productive capacity as workers.
The point is therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the first place to protect the consumer from being inevitably taken advantage of on account of his weakness.
I feel really frustrated, as thousands and thousands of Candians do, by the fact that the problem of consuming and distributing our resources, in a fair, non-socialistic way does not appear on the list of bills men-tionned in the Speech from the Throne.
I feel the same way about the very serious housing problem which is not even alluded to and which is related to consumption.
According to the Social Credit creed, there must be a constant balance between production and consumption, that is to say that at any moment of economic activities, consumption must reach the same level as production.
To serve man, to serve the citizen, all citizens, Mr. Speaker, regardless of race, color, cultural heritage and language, such must be the governing principle of the entire economy.
Any economic system that fails to attain this end does not accomplish its vital function and therefore deserves to be condemned. In judging the actual economic system, I respectfully ask the members of this house if it accomplishes its end with regard to the human beings, to each of the provinces and to Canada as a whole?
So that we may have prosperity and not poverty in the midst of affluence, it is therefore essential that the mechanism of production, consumption, distribution, be cordinated and interconnected so as to fulfil its end, which is the satisfaction of human needs, in a word the establishment of a just society in fact and not only in theory.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne explicitly recognizes that poverty still exists in Canada. It repeats thereby the very interesting statement of the fifth annual report of the Economic Council of Canada. But the Speech from the Throne differs from the latter in that it does not suggest any solution.
It is a fact, poverty exists. But shall we be able to meet the challenge?
Mr. Speaker, in order to impart to the people of Canada the knowledge that, in a country like ours, poverty exists in the midst of
September 17, 1968

plenty, an official report of the Economic Council of Canada-the fifth one-has been necessary.
Previously, when the Creditistes urged the government to take immediate steps in order that the needy might receive bread and butter, the party in power always remained deaf and the newspaper did not bring up the subject. Today, faced with the recommendations of the report, several important personalities and leading newspapermen have shown great surprise at the wide-spread poverty here. And yet, Mr. Speaker, this poverty exists, we see it every day in our midst and sometimes in our own families. Many of our politicians have turned a deaf ear when we tried to tell them about it.
Poverty does not occur suddenly. It is the result of a lack of adequate policies on the part of our leaders for a number of years. The way things are going, one can wonder whether it is not almost too late to avert certain misfortunes or catastrophies which befall these poor families. These people have reached the stage where they feel rejected and almost as if they did not belong to our society. For them, poverty is a sort of insufficient access to some goods, services, and way of life available to all others and considered as essential to a decent standard of living.
For the poor, education, labour movements, spokesmen and associations to represent them and express their views, their yearnings, and their needs are things unknown. Why? Because, on account of their condition, they had to stay away from them. Consequently, they retreated into their humble ghettos, where lack of education, illness, want of money, hunger, cold, isolation, fear-and sometimes crime-touched them and left their stigma on each of them.
What was the government doing in all that, Mr. Speaker? As usual it refused to listen to those who tried to advise it. Of course family allowances, pensions, unemployment insurance benefits were being paid. But what was being done to help the poor help themselves to put them in conditions where they could increase their income, to develop their own possibilities, to improve their circumstances through ther own efforts?
The creditistes had remembered the poor, advocating a guaranteed minimum income for every family. The Prime Minister did not invent the minimum income, Mr. Speaker. They also advocated adjusting family allowances according to the cost of living index, a

The Address-Mr. Perrault health dividend, adequate purchasing power for the consumers, a basic income tax exemption of $3,000 for unmarried people and $5,000 for married people, a maximum interest rate for finance companies which exploit the people, low rental housing and, in co-operation with the various departments and industry, helping the students find summer employment, a guaranteed minimum price for the products of a family farm to ensure the sale of farm products. Those are constructive measures which we expected to find in the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker. Those are only some of the points of the creditiste program to create a just society, and we hope that the Prime Minister will take note of them.
To remedy the problem of poverty, it is necessary first of all to maintain a high employment level; secondly, to get the people interested and somewhat committed to eliminating poverty; thirdly, to direct policies towards the people who need help and not towards those who dispense patronage; fourthly, to maintain incomes and increase the ability of the poor to participate; fifthly, to make economic use of funds and skills to get the most long lasting results for each dollar spent. Will that challenge ever be met, Mr. Speaker, since it is still possible unfortunately to say today that the rich get richer and the poor get poorer? The just society, if it is to be, must first fill this serious gap and without delay. Will the Creditistes be heard this time with a little more attention? We all hope so, for the fate of millions of those poor people will be at stake.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detain the house any longer. I should like to thank you, to congratulate you on your election and to offer you my closest co-operation as member for Lotbiniere. I hope this speech and the debates to follow will be useful to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise for the first time in this house I want to congratulate the mover of the address in reply, the hon. member for Mada-waska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin). The province of New Brunswick has made a remarkable contribution to this nation. The people of New Brunswick have made a contribution totally beyond their numbers within confederation. The province of British Columbia has benefited greatly from the contribution of
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. Perrault people from New Brunswick, although I may say that for more than nine years I have been battling one of its more distinguished sons in the legislature of the province of B.C.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the seconder of the address in reply my good friend and colleague the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand). He will be an able member in his own right. The fact that he is a Canadian of Indian origin adds to the richness of this house, to the diversity and representative character of it.
I congratulate you too, Mr. Speaker, on re-election to the office you hold, because your reputation goes before you. Among those who have served in all the democratic assemblies and legislatures of this nation the Speaker of this house has earned an excellent reputation.
My constituency, Mr. Speaker, is made up of two of the most constructive and progressive areas in the country, and I am grateful to them for the support which they gave me in the recent election. I have the privilege of representing several thousand residents of the municipality of Burnaby, which is the second largest urban area in British Columbia, and as well I represent many of the families of North Vancouver.
We are richly endowed with resources in these areas. We have some fine mountains. May I suggest to the government through you, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to improve communications in this country we should schedule a series of federal cabinet meetings from the Pacific coast to the Atlantic coast so that in the years ahead, the cabinet can meet with every section of this nation, and if the cabinet would like to have a summit conference in North Vancouver on top of one of our mountains we would be glad to play host to it.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
There are thousands of families living in my constituency faced with the problems of families throughout the country. They do not have housing. Too many of them are unemployed for certain periods of the year. They need greater assistance to develop their potential. I intend to advocate measures in all these fields during my period of service in this house. I may have difficulty at times in this assembly. Before I left to come to Ottawa they had a going-away party for me at which the chairman said, "Ray, is it going to be difficult, after serving so long in the opposition, finally to be on the government side?"

Here I am. I am with the government in spirit, but my physical location is still in opposition. If I have a conditioned reflex, a Pavlovian reflex, and I am overly critical- and I hope I am not too unfairly critical of the government at times-it may be because of my position in the house.
I congratulate the opposition parties upon their strenuous efforts to attempt to destroy the speech from the throne. I have been in opposition too long to suggest in any way that the rights and prerogatives of an opposition should be curtailed. No party in this country has a monopoly on good ideas. All the parties in this house have made their contribution. Fair and reasonable opposition is necessary if we are to keep our parliamentary system healthy. Anyone who has experience in opposition must be sympathetic with the problems which confront Her Majesty's opposition when they attempt to stand up and be watchdogs of the people. Laurier said:
I here form part of the people's jury and it is my duty to render a conscientious verdict, regardless of pension or party.
With reference to the speech from the throne the question is, has the verdict been conscientious. I have listened with interest and with some bewilderment to the quality of the opposition which has been advanced during the past few days. The suggestion that this throne speech or any other speech from the throne is supposed to be a complete catalogue of the program of a government is a ludicrous and irresponsible suggestion. This definition of a throne speech is given in "Government of Canada" by Dawson, 1963:
The throne speech reviews the state of the nation and recites in fairly general terms the program which the cabinet proposed to submit to parliament in the coming session.
May I suggest to the opposition that in the review that was given in the speech from the throne there is a foundation program for the coming four years and a belief on the part of the government that before we can create the base the foundation must be such that we can support social reform and pay for advances in all areas. If we attempt to finance the just society on the basis of the base coinage of our inflation, we are courting disaster. In that sense the speech from the throne has been responsible and meets the test of the traditional message from His Excellency. The speech from the throne provides a direction, it provides a pattern for the future. It can only suggest a limited number of areas where
September 17, 1968

government action is anticipated. But when criticism is directed toward the speech from the throne on the basis that it is not specific enough, perhaps the opposition should be reminded of the unprecedented action of the presenting of 47 bills on the very opening day of the session.
There has been a suggestion that the government is indifferent to the problem of those without shelter. Yet even now a task force is commencing its journey from coast to coast in Canada seeking the opinions of people from all political parties and vocations in an effort to obtain the best ideas in order to have a program at the time of the building season at the beginning of the year.
I was bewildered by the quality of the attack on the speech from the throne launched by the leader of Her Majesty's official opposition. He said, as recorded at page 55 of Hansard:
Throughout the speech there is evidence of a lack of a sense of proportion, a preoccupation with legalistic matters, an utterly casual approach insensitive toward economic injustice and the blight of poverty in our land.
There have been other speeches from the throne in other forums and not just in our provincial legislatures-and not all in the province of British Columbia. One speech from the throne was delivered in the Nova Scotia house of assembly in 1967, the last year the right hon. gentleman seated to the left of our flanking group was premier of that province. Let me read into the record the kind of defence entered by that right hon. gentleman when his speech from the throne was brought under attack. These are the words recorded in the Nova Scotia House of Assembly, as they are set down at page 107 of the House of Assembly Debates:
I am sure that any member of the house can present a list of projects which are desirable and important. Any member can stand in his place and say that this should be done and that should be done, but our resources are limited in comparison to the needs to be met, yes, inadequate in comparison to the needs to be met.
I ask hon. members to consider the quality of the opposition by the right hon. gentleman the other day and compare his remarks then with his defence in 1967 in his own legislature when he was endowed with responsibility. Then he continued:
We are certainly not meeting all of the needs, but we have tried to allocate the resources that are available toward the most pressing needs in an effort to produce the most beneficial results that we can offer our province and its people.
The Address-Mr. Perrault
Those words are somewhat reminiscent of some of the language in the speech from the throne we have before us. Has the hon. gentleman's philosophy altered during that intervening time?
We have a similar situation with regard to the members of the New Democratic party. I am familiar with some of them. The attack launched by the members of the New Democratic party in this house was an attack by a group enjoying the luxury of an opposition which has the positive knowledge they will never be called upon to form a government in this Canada of ours. But there was a time when they were empowered with the responsibility of government. I had the privilege and pleasure of attending the convention of the Saskatchewan Federation of Labour the last year the C.C.F. governed the great province of Saskatchewan. We are told in this house that today the New Democratic party believes that through planning we can bring about full employment in this nation; yet I have never in my life heard a more bitter indictment of any government than the indictment in 1962 by the Saskatchewan Federation of Labour of the C.C.F. because of their failure to fight unemployment.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Again vested with power and responsibility these opposition parties demonstrated a different philosophy and a singular lack of success in providing neat, pat solutions to the major problems which beset this nation. This reminds me of a baseball manager I spoke with last summer. His team was in a 13 game losing streak. He said it was very difficult to go to the baseball stadium every night when the fans were yelling down to put in a new pitcher, and asking why someone was not getting a hit or why the team was making so many errors. His comment was that, while up in the stands every fan was a 30 game winner with a batting average of 350, and might never make a field error, one could not coax them down on to the field.
I am glad to note that in this throne speech we are anticipating and contemplating parliamentary reforms which will enable any member of the opposition in this house with a good idea to contribute that idea effectively to the standing committees of the house. Not only that, such a member will be financed in the process. If any ideas exist among members of the opposition, and I am sure that there are many, this government will give the members a chance to put those ideas over.
September 17, 1968

The Address-Mr. Perraulc Some of these 350 hitters will have a chance to get up to bat.
Anyone who listened to the speech from the throne with any degree of detachment heard, first of all, an acceptance of responsibility for the leadership which has been bestowed by the people of Canada on this government. This was not a speech festooned with piecrust promises not possible of fulfilment. We were told we must marshal our intellectual and financial resources and that priorities must be established. We were told that a firm foundation for the future must be established during this first session of the twenty eighth parliament. That foundation is going to include procedural reforms.
We have been told in effect that we cannot run a $12 billion corporation along business lines established in the 1880's, and that is one [DOT]of the reasons the government advocates parliamentary reform. We have been told that procedural reform is a priority matter because the volume of work to be handled by this house is to be such that improved procedures are imperative.
We have also been told that national unity is a priority and that appropriate action is to be taken to strengthen and improve confederation. We in western Canada have made progress. This is one of the most rapidly growing provinces in Canada and we are as concerned .about national unity as we are about economic growth.
British Columbians of all parties love their province and their country, and no one has a monopoly in this respect. Centennial year intensified our love for our nation. We respect vhe commonwealth and we respect the institutions which the commonwealth represents. The 16 members from British Columbia look upon our presence here, at least in part, as an opportunity to strengthen the bonds of confederation and to play a constructive role in building a new and better future for Canada.
The history of our province and its development since we entered confederation is one of a progressive people who have progressed, not because they have been standing unalterably across the highway blocking progress or by gazing nostalgically into the past refusing to act, but because they believe that times are changing and that the nation is changing. We are prepared to demonstrate that this nation has in that specific province a strong western bastion of confederation. We hope to assist in the intelligent and reasoned consideration of

confederation and the constitution, as well as ways to improve both. The vast majority of us want to join every national dialogue about Canada's future because we believe that much of Canada's future lies in this province and in the west.
We have much to offer that dialogue. British Columbia is the fastest growing province in the nation. It is a wealthy province with a great fund of human and physical resources. The settling of our province was accomplished by co-operating, hard-working racially diverse people drawn from every Canadian province and from throughout the world, who came here and together conquered the wilderness. Whether they stepped ashore, or arrived from overland like my ancestors, they were met by individuals like the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo.
In British Columbia we have a diverse racial culture, we are united and we have something to say to the rest of Canada about unity. If we do not understand completely the French-English dialogue perhaps it is because we have been building a future in the most difficult geographical area in Canada. Perhaps we have had insufficient time to ponder this question.
The issue today as far as British Columbians are concerned does not involve French Canada or English Canada but rather an unhyphenated Canada. Our concern cannot be related to the linguistic and cultural future of Canada alone: it involves very much Canada's economic future as well. Without a strong economy, cultural institutions of any kind have little chance of growing and developing.

The province of British Columbia was settled by people of all races, faiths and philosophical tendencies. The first ties binding us to Canada were woven by people coming from Asia. By the thousand they contributed, through their labour and sometimes by sacrificing their life, to the construction of a railway connecting us with the rest of Canada.
These people came from all over the world and from the other provinces, seeking a higher standard of living.
The co-operation of all those groups was necessary to overcome all the obstacles met in the wilderness which was then British Columbia. The citizens of British Columbia are now proud and happy of the progress made.
September 17, 1968

Some of those who claim that they are speaking for our provinces seem to think that there is an impassable stone wall between British Columbia and the remainder of Canada.
I would like to tell the house, Mr. Chairman, that the record number of Liberal members from British Columbia elected to the Canadian Parliament bears out the fact that the people of British Columbia are no introverts, scowling behind a stone wall.
The great majority of citizens in British Columbia believe in the future of Canada and are ready to strengthen the ties of Confederation and make all necessary adjustments which could be required in the process.
Much has been said about the language rights of the two founding races. Some are afraid of being forced to speak English or obliged to speak French; but in Canada as it is today, and more and more in the Canada of tomorrow, I want my children to be bilingual, indeed I would like them to be able to express themselves in many languages, the more so since they will have to live in a shrinking world, a world in which progress will depend upon the knowledge of other languages, other cultures and other peoples. [English]
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian of tomorrow should know English, French and as many other languages as he can assimilate. He will be a better Canadian for it and a better world citizen.
If there is a sufficient number of French speaking citizens in any area of Canada who want their children to be educated in French as a primary language, by all means let us grant them that right. At the same time let us encourage them, for the sake of their children, to develop the greatest possible fluency in English as well as in French.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Canadians have everything to lose and nothing to gain by relying on alleged historical, statistical and legalistic precedents to deny their neighbours cultural and linguistic equality. Canada has made more progress in its brief 100 years of existence than any other nation in the world. We have not made all that progress in this brief period of time by opposing change, innovation and reform.
